course.title: Music Theory
course.description: Read and understand the notes, scales, intervals, rhythms and chords behind the music you hear, and see why they fit together.
course.audience: A curious adult who listens to music and may play a little by ear or by chord chart, but cannot read notation or explain why a chord progression works. Needs arithmetic and counting only. No instrument required; a keyboard or guitar helps.

paragraphs: Every note you hear is a vibration, and the A near the middle of a piano, which orchestras tune to, vibrates 440 times a second. Play the A keys up the keyboard and you hear the same note again and again, each one higher, and the keys between any two of them are a fixed set of evenly spaced steps that the ear hears as equal. Most of the music you know is built from those steps. A scale is a choice of some of them and a chord is a few of them sounded together, so both can be described exactly by counting steps and letter names, and the same is true of intervals and keys.

Music theory is that description, and it is useful because it explains things we already hear. We can tell that a chord wants to move on, or that a minor key sounds different from a major one, long before we can say why, and theory lets us point at the notes responsible. It also gives us a common way of writing music down and talking about it, so that a phrase on the page can be read and played by someone who has never heard it.
outcomes: You'll be able to read single notes on treble and bass clef and name them by pitch.
You'll be able to build any major scale and the three minor scales from their step patterns, and name a key from its signature.
You'll be able to name an interval by number and quality and work out its size in semitones.
You'll be able to count and notate rhythm in simple and compound metre.
You'll be able to build triads and seventh chords, label them with Roman numerals and explain common progressions and cadences.
You'll be able to spot parallel fifths and octaves, fix them in four-part writing, and describe the form of a short piece.

modules.title: Pitch and notation
modules.description: What a note is, how pitches are named, and how notes are written on a staff.

modules.title: Scales, keys and intervals
modules.description: The step patterns that make scales, the signatures that name keys, and the interval as the measure of distance between notes.

modules.title: Rhythm and metre
modules.description: How time is divided into beats and bars and written down.

modules.title: Harmony, voice leading and form
modules.description: Chords built from scales, why progressions pull toward home, how voices move together, and how phrases build a piece.

concepts.title: Pitch
concepts.summary: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds, and it corresponds to the frequency of the vibration in hertz.

concepts.title: Octave
concepts.summary: Two notes an octave apart have the same letter name and a frequency ratio of exactly 2:1.

concepts.title: Semitone
concepts.summary: A semitone is the distance from one key to the nearest key above or below it, black or white; there are 12 in an octave.

concepts.title: Equal temperament
concepts.summary: In equal temperament each semitone multiplies frequency by 2^(1/12), about 1.05946, so 12 of them make a doubling.

concepts.title: Staff
concepts.summary: The staff is five lines with four spaces, and each line or space stands for one letter name; higher on the staff means higher in pitch.

concepts.title: Clef
concepts.summary: A clef fixes which line or space is which pitch: the treble clef curls round G4, the bass clef marks F3 between its two dots.

concepts.title: Ledger line
concepts.summary: A short extra line drawn through or beside a note head extends the staff, as for middle C.

concepts.title: Middle C
concepts.summary: Middle C, C4, sits on the first ledger line below the treble staff and the first ledger line above the bass staff.

concepts.title: Accidental
concepts.summary: A sharp raises a note by a semitone, a flat lowers it by a semitone, and a natural cancels an earlier sharp or flat.

concepts.title: Enharmonic equivalent
concepts.summary: Two spellings of the same key, such as F-sharp and G-flat, are enharmonic equivalents.

concepts.title: Whole tone
concepts.summary: A whole tone is two semitones; between neighbouring white keys it spans a black key, except at E-F and B-C.

concepts.title: Chromatic scale
concepts.summary: The chromatic scale uses all 12 semitones in an octave.

concepts.title: Major scale
concepts.summary: A major scale is seven notes built from the step pattern W W H W W W H, returning to the starting letter an octave higher.

concepts.title: Scale degree
concepts.summary: Each note of a scale has a number 1 to 7 and a name: tonic, supertonic, mediant, subdominant, dominant, submediant, leading tone.

concepts.title: Tonic
concepts.summary: The tonic is the first degree, the note the scale and key are named after and the one that feels like home.

concepts.title: Interval number
concepts.summary: The number of an interval counts letter names from the lower note to the upper note, inclusive, so C up to E is a third.

concepts.title: Interval quality
concepts.summary: Quality (perfect, major, minor, augmented, diminished) says which of the possible sizes the number takes.

concepts.title: Compound interval
concepts.summary: An interval larger than an octave is compound and is named by adding 7 to the simple number, so an octave and a third is a tenth.

concepts.title: Inversion
concepts.summary: Turning an interval upside down changes its number n to 9 - n and swaps major with minor and augmented with diminished, but keeps perfect perfect.

concepts.title: Key signature
concepts.summary: A key signature lists the sharps or flats of the key at the start of every staff, so they need not be written on each note.

concepts.title: Circle of fifths
concepts.summary: Going up a perfect fifth from C adds one sharp each time; going down a fifth adds one flat; after 12 steps you are back at C.

concepts.title: Relative minor
concepts.summary: The relative minor shares its major key's signature and starts a minor third (3 semitones) below the major tonic.

concepts.title: Natural minor
concepts.summary: Natural minor follows the step pattern W H W W H W W and uses its relative major's signature.

concepts.title: Harmonic minor
concepts.summary: Harmonic minor raises the seventh degree of natural minor by a semitone, so the leading tone pulls to the tonic.

concepts.title: Melodic minor
concepts.summary: Ascending melodic minor raises both the sixth and seventh degrees; the descending form usually returns to natural minor.

concepts.title: Parallel key
concepts.summary: Parallel keys share a tonic but not a signature, such as C major and C minor.

concepts.title: Beat and tempo
concepts.summary: The beat is the steady pulse and tempo counts beats per minute, so one beat lasts 60 / bpm seconds.

concepts.title: Time signature
concepts.summary: The top number gives beats per bar and the bottom number gives the note value of one beat, so 3/4 is three quarter-note beats.

concepts.title: Note value
concepts.summary: A whole note lasts four quarter-note beats, a half note two, a quarter one, an eighth half a beat; a dot adds half of the note's own value.

concepts.title: Compound metre
concepts.summary: In compound metre each beat divides into three, so 6/8 feels like two beats of three eighth notes.

concepts.title: Syncopation
concepts.summary: Syncopation puts emphasis where the metre does not expect it, often by tying across a strong beat or by resting on it.

concepts.title: Triad
concepts.summary: A triad is three notes stacked in thirds: root, third and fifth.

concepts.title: Chord quality
concepts.summary: A major triad is a major third plus a minor third (4 + 3 semitones), a minor triad 3 + 4, a diminished triad 3 + 3 and an augmented triad 4 + 4.

concepts.title: Diatonic triads
concepts.summary: Stacking thirds on each degree of the major scale gives major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished: I ii iii IV V vi vii-dim.

concepts.title: Dominant seventh
concepts.summary: Add a minor seventh above the root of a major triad and the chord is a dominant seventh, such as G B D F.

concepts.title: Chord inversion
concepts.summary: A chord is in root position when its root is the lowest note; first inversion has the third lowest, second inversion has the fifth lowest.

concepts.title: Harmonic function
concepts.summary: Chords act as tonic (home, I), predominant (leaving home, ii or IV) or dominant (tension, V or vii-dim) and tend to move in that order.

concepts.title: Cadence
concepts.summary: A cadence is a chord pair that ends a phrase: authentic V-I, half cadence ending on V, plagal IV-I and deceptive V-vi.

concepts.title: Tritone resolution
concepts.summary: The third and seventh of V7 form a tritone, 6 semitones, which resolves inward to the root and third of I.

concepts.title: Leading tone
concepts.summary: The leading tone is the seventh degree, a semitone below the tonic, and tends to rise to it.

concepts.title: Types of motion
concepts.summary: Voices move in parallel (same interval), similar (same direction), oblique (one holds) or contrary (opposite directions).

concepts.title: Parallel fifths and octaves
concepts.summary: Two voices a perfect fifth or octave apart that move to another perfect fifth or octave in the same direction sound like a single voice and are avoided in common-practice writing.

concepts.title: Common-tone retention
concepts.summary: Where two chords share a note, keeping it in the same voice makes a smooth join.

concepts.title: Voice ranges
concepts.summary: Soprano, alto, tenor and bass each occupy a range of about an octave and a half and should stay close.

concepts.title: Phrase
concepts.summary: A phrase is a musical thought that ends at a cadence, often four bars long.

concepts.title: Period
concepts.summary: A period is two phrases, an antecedent ending on a weaker cadence and a consequent ending on a stronger one, usually eight bars.

concepts.title: Sectional form
concepts.summary: Binary (AB), ternary (ABA), rondo (ABACA) and verse-chorus layouts describe how sections are arranged and repeated.

concepts.title: Twelve-bar blues
concepts.summary: The blues is twelve bars of I, IV and V chords: four of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, I (or V).

concepts.title: Sonata form
concepts.summary: Sonata form has an exposition presenting two themes, a development that transforms them and a recapitulation returning both in the home key.

lessons.title: Pitch and the keyboard

lead.text: Look at a piano keyboard and the first thing you notice is a pattern: the white keys are named by the seven letters A to G, which then start again, and the black keys fall into alternating groups of two and three. Find a group of two black keys, put your eye on the white key immediately to its left, and that key is always **C**.
The letters run upward to the right, C D E F G A B, and then another C begins the next round. We call the distance from one C to the next an **octave**.

diagram.caption: White keys carry seven letters that repeat. The black keys come in groups of two and three, which lets you find C by sight. Use the buttons to switch the view.

lead.text: When you press a piano key, a string vibrates back and forth some number of times each second, and we measure that count in **hertz** (Hz), where 1 Hz is one vibration per second. The higher the frequency, the higher the note sounds to us, and we call this quality of a sound its **pitch**.

To name a note exactly we also need to say which octave it is in, so musicians number the octaves and write the number after the letter. The C near the middle of a piano is C4, the A just above it is A4, and the note A4 has a standard frequency of **440 Hz**. That value was fixed by an international standard, ISO 16, first issued in 1955 and confirmed in 1975; before that the A used by orchestras differed from place to place and from decade to decade.

reveal.text: The next screen gives the rule that links the two frequencies.

lead.text: Each A on the keyboard has twice the frequency of the A below it, so going up the keyboard from A2 the As are 110, 220, 440, 880 and 1760 Hz. We call this relationship an **octave**: two notes an octave apart have a frequency **ratio of 2 to 1**. That is why they sound like the same note at different heights, and why they share a letter name.

What matters here is that the relationship is a ratio and not a difference. From 110 to 220 Hz is a rise of 110, and from 880 to 1760 Hz is a rise of 880, yet our ears hear both as exactly one octave. So if you ever want the frequency of a note an octave away, you multiply or divide by 2 and never add a fixed amount.

afterFigure.text: The second view of the figure is drawn so that equal ratios get equal heights. You can see that the five As rise in even steps, which is how the ear hears them, even though in hertz the steps get larger and larger.

diagram.alt: Five bars for the frequencies of A2 to A6, 110, 220, 440, 880 and 1760 hertz. On a linear axis the bars grow faster and faster. On a logarithmic axis they rise in equal steps.
diagram.caption: The same five As on two scales. On the linear axis each octave adds more height than the last, while on the logarithmic axis every octave adds the same height. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Going down an octave halves the frequency, and the same halving works from A2 onward: 55 Hz, then 27.5 Hz.
The next screen gives that step a name and shows where the count comes from.

lead.text: Pick any key, black or white, and look at its nearest neighbour above. The step between them is the smallest step on a piano, and we call it a **semitone**. Counting from one C to the next, there are 12 semitones, which is why the octave is built from twelve keys even though it carries only seven letter names. The word *octave* means eighth, because it counts the letters from C to the next C with both ends included, so the name tells you about the letters and not about the steps.

Most pairs of neighbouring white keys have a black key between them, so they are two semitones apart, but E and F touch, and so do B and C, so those two pairs are only one semitone apart. The uneven look of the keyboard is only the white keys fitting the twelve even steps, and the black keys fill the gaps that are left.

diagram.alt: A keyboard from C4 to C5 with a number under each key counting semitones from the first C, from 0 to 12, and a second view marking the two places where two white keys touch.
diagram.caption: Counting every key, black and white, takes 12 steps from one C to the next. Between E and F, and between B and C, the white keys touch, so those steps are single semitones.

steps.headline: Count the semitones from D4 up to A4.

workedSteps.text: Start on D and go up one key at a time, counting each step whether it lands on a black key or a white one. The first step goes to the black key just above D.
The next step reaches E, a white key, and E is touching F, so the step after that goes straight to F without a black key between.
Above F there is a black key, then G, then another black key, and then A, and the count carries on from the 3 at F.
Counting the steps gives the distance from D4 to A4.

lead.text: We said an octave doubles the frequency and holds twelve semitones. If every semitone is the same size in the way the ear hears it, each one must multiply the frequency by the same number, and twelve of those multiplications must make 2. That number is the twelfth root of 2, written 2^(1/12) and equal to about **1.05946**. This tuning, where the twelve steps are exactly equal in ratio, is called **equal temperament**, and it is how pianos and most keyboards are tuned today.

So the frequency of the key n semitones above A4 is 440 × 2^(n/12), and a negative n goes below it. E5 is 7 semitones above A4, which gives 440 × 2^(7/12) = 659.26 Hz. Middle C is 9 semitones below, and 440 × 2^(−9/12) = 261.63 Hz. Notice that 659.26 sits very close to 660, which is 3/2 of 440. A rise of 220 Hz above 440 Hz therefore lands about seven semitones up, and the next octave would need a rise of 440 Hz.

afterFigure.text: In the second view of the figure, the midpoint of 440 and 880 Hz by simple addition is 660 Hz, but that note is seven steps up and not six. The ear measures a step by the ratio, so the halfway note in pitch is the one reached after six equal multiplications, about 622 Hz.

diagram.alt: A row of thirteen keys from A4 to A5, numbered 0 to 12 with their frequencies from 440 to 880 hertz. One view shows each step multiplying the frequency by about 1.0595. The other shows that 660 hertz, the halfway point by addition, falls seven steps up and not six.

lessons.orientation: Count semitones between keys and find the frequency of a note from A4 = 440 Hz.
lessons.nextAction: Read the name and octave of a note on the treble or bass staff.

blocks.text: On a piano the A near the middle vibrates 440 times each second. Play it and then the next A up the keyboard, and you hear the same note again, higher but plainly the same, which is why the keyboard gives both keys the letter A. The higher A is vibrating at a different rate, though, and so is every key between the two, each one a little faster than the key below it.
What links the rate of one A to the rate of the next, and how much faster is each key than its neighbour?

intro.whyItMatters: Every scale, interval and chord in this course is a pattern of semitones, so counting them is the first skill.

recap.keyIdea: Pitch follows frequency, an octave is a doubling, and the keyboard divides the octave into twelve equal semitone steps.

blocks.text: You counted twelve semitones from one C to the next, and you saw that the name *octave* counts letters and not steps. Because the ear hears ratios, each octave doubles the frequency, and in equal temperament each semitone multiplies it by 2^(1/12), so 440 × 2^(n/12) gives the key n semitones from A4.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson puts these notes on five lines and reads them from the page.

lessons.title: The staff and clefs

lead.text: Music is written on a **staff** of five horizontal lines, which gives four spaces between them. Each line and each space stands for one of the letters, and the letters climb in order as you move up, so a note placed higher on the staff is a higher pitch. By itself, though, the staff cannot say *which* letter a given line is, and that is the job of the symbol at its left end, the **clef**.

The treble clef is drawn so that its curl circles the second line from the bottom, and that line is G4. Once we know one line, we know the rest, because the letters go in order: the space just below G4 is F4, and the line below that, the bottom line, is E4. Going up from G4 works the same way, one letter for each line or space, and the octave number goes up by one each time the count passes from B to C.

diagram.alt: A treble staff with nine whole notes from the bottom line to the top line, with only E4 on the bottom line and G4 on the clef's line labelled, and the same for a bass staff with only G2 on the bottom line and F3 on the clef's line labelled. lead.text: Low notes written on the treble staff would need many ledger lines, short extra lines drawn below the staff for notes that fall off it, so a second clef is used for them. The **bass clef** is anchored on the fourth line from the bottom, which sits between the clef's two dots, and that line is F3. Its bottom line is G2, and every other line and space is found by counting letters up or down from F3, exactly as on the treble staff, which makes the top line A3.
Notice that the bottom line of the treble staff is E4 while the bottom line of the bass staff is G2, so a note head on that line is a different letter *and* a different octave in the two clefs.

afterFigure.text: Reading a note in the wrong clef is the most common slip in the first weeks, so the habit that matters is to look at the clef before you look at the note.

reveal.text: The next screen shows where those notes are written, and why one of them gets its own short line.

lead.text: The letters between A3 and E4 are B3, C4 and D4. The staves do not have room for them, so we add a short line through or beside the note head, called a **ledger line**, which acts as a temporary extension of the staff. Ledger lines are counted *away from the staff* in the direction of the note, so the first one below the treble staff is C4 and the first one above the bass staff is also C4.

That note is **middle C**, written C4, and it is the pitch that links the two staves. When a composer joins both staves with a line at the left, we call the pair a **grand staff**, the usual layout for keyboard music, with the right hand mostly on the treble and the left on the bass.

diagram.alt: Middle C, C4, written three ways: on a ledger line below the treble staff, on a ledger line above the bass staff, and in both staves of a grand staff joined by a brace line.
diagram.caption: A ledger line extends the staff by one step. Counting away from the staff, middle C is one ledger line below the treble staff and one ledger line above the bass staff.

steps.headline: Find the note in the fourth space of the treble staff by counting from the G line.

workedSteps.text: Start from the one line you know. The treble clef circles the second line from the bottom, so that line is G4.
Move up one step at a time, alternating space and line, and take the next letter each time.
workedSteps.math: space A4, line B4, space C5, line D5

workedSteps.text: The fourth space from the bottom is the next step after D5. Name it, with its octave.

steps.headline: Find the note in the second space of the bass staff by counting down from the F line.

workedSteps.text: The bass clef marks the fourth line from the bottom, which is F3. This time we are going down, so the letters run backward.
Moving down one step at a time gives the space below, then the line below that.
The next step down is the second space from the bottom. Name it, with its octave.

reveal.text: Counting from a known note, such as the bottom line E4, works for any distance, inside the staff or out of it.

lessons.orientation: Read the name and octave of a single note on the treble or bass staff, including middle C.
lessons.nextAction: Write the black-key notes with sharps and flats, and tell enharmonic spellings apart.

blocks.text: Here is a single note head on the second line of a five-line staff. We can't name it yet, because the same position stands for two different notes depending on a small symbol at the start of the line, and a player who ignores that symbol will play a note more than an octave away from the one written.
That symbol is the **clef**, and it ties one line of the staff to one exact note.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read the name and octave of a single note on the treble or bass staff, and find middle C in both.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later lesson writes its examples on a staff, so reading one note quickly comes first.

recap.keyIdea: A clef fixes which line is which pitch, and the notes are named by counting up or down from the line it marks.

blocks.text: The treble clef circles G4 on its second line and the bass clef marks F3 on its fourth, which is why one position on the staff means two different notes. Because ledger lines carry the staff outward, middle C, C4, can be written below the treble staff or above the bass staff, and counting from a note you know is faster than reciting the letters from the bottom.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson adds the black keys to the page with sharps and flats.

lessons.title: Sharps, flats and the semitone

steps.headline: Whole tones and the chromatic scale

lead.text: Most pairs of neighbouring white keys have a black key between them, which makes the step between them two semitones, and we call a step of two semitones a **whole tone**. The exceptions are E to F and B to C, which touch, so each of those is a single semitone.

If we play every key from one C to the next, in order, black and white, we use all twelve semitones. We call that sequence the **chromatic scale**, and it will serve us as a ruler, since any distance on the keyboard can be measured by counting the steps of the chromatic scale.

diagram.alt: A keyboard from C4 to C5. One view names the five black keys with a sharp name and a flat name each. The other brackets the white keys C and D as a whole tone of two semitones and E and F as a single semitone.
diagram.caption: The twelve keys of an octave are the chromatic scale. Between most white neighbours there is a black key, so the step is a whole tone, and E to F and B to C are single semitones.

reveal.text: The next screen names the black keys that appeared in that count.

lead.text: The five black keys have no letters of their own, so we name each one from the white key beside it. The black key just above F is one semitone higher than F, and we write that with a **sharp**, F♯. The black key just below B is one semitone lower than B, and a **flat** writes that as B♭. A third sign, the **natural**, written ♮, cancels a sharp or a flat that is still in force, and brings the note back to its plain letter. We call all three signs **accidentals**.

On the staff an accidental goes before the note head it changes, on the same line or space. Once you have written it, the change holds for the rest of that bar for every note on that line or space, and it ends at the barline.

diagram.alt: A treble staff showing four cases: a sharp sign raising F4 to F sharp, a flat sign lowering B4 to B flat, a natural sign cancelling a sharp, and a sharp that carries on through the rest of the bar and ends at the barline.
diagram.caption: Accidentals are written before the note head they change. Use the buttons to see each one.

reveal.text: Notice that the flat lowers the note by a semitone and moves it to the black key on the left.

lead.text: Since a sharp comes from the white key below and a flat from the white key above, every black key has two names. The black key between F and G is F♯, a semitone above F, and also G♭, a semitone below G. We call two spellings of the same key **enharmonic equivalents**. They sound the same on a keyboard, and the choice between them is about the notation, so that a scale uses each letter name once and the page stays easy to read.

White keys can have a second name as well. E♯ raises E by a semitone, which lands on F, and C♭ lowers C by a semitone, which lands on B, since E and F touch and so do B and C. So a flat is not always a black key, and a sharp is not always a black key either. A sharp or a flat names a *step*, and it is the position of that step on the keyboard that decides whether the key is black or white.

afterFigure.text: The three views each light a single key. In each case two names point at it, and the keyboard cannot tell the names apart.

reveal.text: Notice the pattern: the sharp name counts up from the lower letter and the flat name counts down from the upper one.
The same reasoning gives E♯ = F, a white key named by a sharp.

steps.headline: Count the semitones from F♯ up to C by stepping along the chromatic scale.

workedSteps.text: Start on F♯ and take the chromatic scale one key at a time. The first key above F♯ is G, a white key.
Then the black key above G, which is G♯ or A♭, and the white key A.
Then the black key above A, and the white key B.
B and C touch, so the next step lands straight on C. Give the total.

steps.headline: Count the semitones from B♭ up to F in the same way.

workedSteps.text: Start on B♭, a black key. The first key above it is the white key B.
B and C touch, so the next step is C, and then the black key above it.
Then D, D♯, E, and finally F, because E and F touch. Give the total from B♭ to F.

reveal.text: Check by counting in the other direction: A down to F is also 4 semitones.

lessons.orientation: Raise or lower a note with accidentals, find where no black key sits, and give an enharmonic spelling.
lessons.nextAction: Build the major scale from the pattern of whole tones and semitones.

blocks.text: Press the white key F on a piano and then the black key just above it, and the second note is higher by the smallest step the keyboard has. Look for that black key in printed music and you'll find it written in two ways, sometimes as F♯ and sometimes as G♭, although it is the same key and sounds exactly the same.
Why does music keep two names for one key? Each of those small signs moves a note up or down by one semitone, so F♯ is F raised and G♭ is G lowered, and the two land on the same key.

intro.promise: By the end you'll raise or lower a note with accidentals, spot where the keyboard has no black key, and give an enharmonic spelling.
intro.whyItMatters: Scales and key signatures are built from these signs, so reading them comes before either.

recap.keyIdea: A sharp or flat moves a note one semitone, so every key can be spelled in more than one way, and counting along the chromatic scale measures any distance.

blocks.text: You saw that a whole tone is two semitones except at E to F and B to C, that a sharp raises and a flat lowers a note by one semitone, and that a natural cancels either. Two spellings of one key are called enharmonic equivalents, which is why E♯ is a white key and C♭ is too. To measure a distance, name the keys you are starting and ending on and count the chromatic steps between them.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses whole tones and semitones in a fixed pattern to build the major scale.

lessons.title: The major scale

lead.text: Play the white keys from one C to the next and you hear a **scale**, a stepwise run of notes that ends where it began, an octave higher. That particular scale is C major, and its first note, C, is called the **tonic**, the note the scale is named after and the one that sounds like home. The other notes lean toward it.

What defines the scale is the sequence of steps. Going up from C, the distances are whole tone, whole tone, half step, whole tone, whole tone, whole tone, half step, where a **half step** is another name for a semitone, and we write the pattern **W W H W W W H**. The two half steps are where the white keys touch: E to F and B to C, which are the third-to-fourth and seventh-to-eighth steps of the scale.

afterFigure.text: The second view of the figure shows the steps. Because we've counted it in semitones, the total is 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 12, the octave from Lesson 1.

diagram.alt: A keyboard from C4 to C5 with the eight keys of C major highlighted, which are all the white keys. In the second view the steps between them are marked W for whole tone and H for semitone, giving W W H W W W H.
diagram.caption: C major uses the white keys. The two semitone steps fall between the third and fourth notes and between the seventh and eighth.

reveal.text: The next screen carries this out on three different starting notes.

lead.text: Start on G and apply the pattern. G to A is a whole tone, A to B is a whole tone, B to C is a half step, C to D and D to E are whole tones, and then comes E to the next note, which must be a whole tone. The white key after E is F, only a semitone away, so we have to use the black key F♯, and then a half step takes us to G. The sharp is not an extra: it is there to keep the pattern, and the pattern is what makes it a major scale.

So C major isn't *the* scale with the others as variants. It uses only white keys because of the way the keyboard happens to be drawn, and every major scale has the same shape. D major starts on D and needs F♯ and C♯, and E major needs four sharps. We also spell each scale so that every letter name appears once, which is why the black keys in B♭ major are B♭ and E♭ and not A♯ and D♯: the scale already has an A and a D.

diagram.alt: Three keyboards, each with a major scale highlighted and the steps between its notes marked W or H. G major from G4 to G5 uses F sharp. D major from D4 to D5 uses F sharp and C sharp. E major from E4 to E5 uses F sharp, G sharp, C sharp and D sharp.
diagram.caption: The same pattern W W H W W W H, started on three different notes. Each scale has to use black keys in different places to keep the pattern.

reveal.text: Notice that a white key can come up in a scale that is full of sharps.

lead.text: We number the notes of a scale from 1 to 7, and the eighth is the tonic again, an octave up. Each degree also has a traditional name: **tonic** (1), **supertonic** (2), **mediant** (3), **subdominant** (4), **dominant** (5), **submediant** (6) and **leading tone** (7). The names that matter most are the tonic, the dominant, which is the fifth degree and the strongest support for the tonic, and the leading tone, which sits a semitone below the tonic and pulls upward into it.
From the tonic to the submediant is W W H W W, which is 9 semitones, and from degree 7 to degree 8 is always one semitone.

diagram.alt: The major scale written on a treble staff. In C major the notes run C4 to C5 and in D major D4 to D5 with F sharp and C sharp. Under each note is its letter name and its degree number 1 to 8, and the two half steps are bracketed between degrees 3 and 4 and between 7 and 8.
diagram.caption: In every major scale the half steps come between degrees 3 and 4 and between degrees 7 and 8. Use the buttons to compare two scales.

steps.headline: Build A major from A, one step at a time, using each letter name once.

workedSteps.text: The letters run A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and the pattern is W W H W W W H. A to B is a whole tone, and B is two semitones above A.
B to C would be one semitone, but the pattern wants a whole tone, so the third note is the black key above C.
C♯ to D is a half step, as the pattern asks, and then D to E and E to F♯ are whole tones.
workedSteps.math: A B C♯ D E F♯

workedSteps.text: The next step is a whole tone above F♯, which lands on a black key before the final half step back to A. Name the seventh note.

steps.headline: Build F major with each letter used once.

workedSteps.text: The letters are F, G, A, B, C, D, E. F to G is a whole tone and G to A is a whole tone, so both are plain white keys.
The third step of the pattern is a half step, from A to the fourth letter. Give the fourth note in words, keeping the letter B.
The remaining notes are C, D and E, all white keys, and E to F is the closing half step.
workedSteps.math: F G A B♭ C D E F

reveal.text: Your answer has to sit a semitone below the tonic, and the scale you built tells you which note that is.

lessons.orientation: Build a major scale on any note from W W H W W W H and name its degrees.
lessons.nextAction: Name the distance between two notes as an interval, with a number and a quality.

blocks.text: Play the white keys from C up to the next C and the run sounds finished, like a tune that has arrived home. Start the same run of white keys on D and it sounds slightly wrong, because the last note doesn't land the way the C did. Nothing has changed except the starting key, so something in the *spacing* between the keys must be what made the run from C sound right.

What is it about that spacing, and can we reproduce it starting from any other note? The answer is a fixed pattern of whole and half steps, and with it we can build a scale that sounds like the run from C on any of the twelve keys, sharps and flats included, and give each of its notes a name.

intro.promise: By the end you'll build a major scale on any starting note from the pattern W W H W W W H, and name its degrees.
intro.whyItMatters: The major scale is the ruler for keys, intervals and chords in the rest of the course.

recap.keyIdea: A major scale is the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half from any starting note, with each letter name used once.

blocks.text: C major happens to need only white keys. Starting on G, D, E or A, the same pattern calls for sharps, and starting on F it calls for B♭, so every major scale has the same shape in a different place. We number its degrees 1 to 7 and name them from tonic to leading tone, with half steps always between degrees 3 and 4 and between 7 and 8.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson measures the distance between any two notes and names it as an interval.

lessons.title: Intervals

lead.text: The distance between two notes is called an **interval**, and its first piece of information is a number. To find it, count the letter names from the lower note up to the upper one, starting with the lower note as 1. From C up to E the letters are C, D, E, so the interval is a **third**; from C up to G they are C, D, E, F, G, so it is a **fifth**.
Notice that we are counting *letters* here, and not steps between them or semitones. The number tells us how far apart the notes are on the staff, and the size on the keyboard is a separate question.

diagram.alt: A treble staff with the notes of the letters counted one at a time. From C to E the count is 1, 2, 3, a third. From C to G the count is 5, a fifth. From C to B the count is 7, a seventh.
diagram.caption: The number of an interval is the count of letter names from the lower note to the upper, with both ends included. Use the buttons to compare three counts.

reveal.text: The next screen explains why two thirds can be different sizes.

lead.text: The major scale supplies a reference. Measured from its first note, the second degree is 2 semitones away, the third 4, the fourth 5, the fifth 7, the sixth 9, the seventh 11 and the octave 12. An interval whose size matches the major scale is a **major** interval for the seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths, and a **perfect** interval for the unison, fourth, fifth and octave. Lower a major interval by a semitone and it becomes **minor**. D up to F is a minor third because it is 3 semitones, one fewer than the 4 of a major third.

Go further and the other two qualities appear. Raise a major or perfect interval by a semitone and it is **augmented**. Lower a perfect interval by a semitone, or a minor interval by one, and it is **diminished**. So there are four kinds of third (diminished, minor, major and augmented, at 2, 3, 4 and 5 semitones) but only three kinds of fifth (diminished, perfect and augmented, at 6, 7 and 8). Perfect intervals have no major and minor forms, which is why nobody speaks of a major fourth.

afterFigure.text: Use the buttons to move from the reference sizes to the thirds and the fifths. In every case the quality says how far an interval sits from the major-scale size for its number.

Another shows the four kinds of third, from the diminished third at 2 semitones to the augmented third at 5. The last shows the three kinds of fifth, at 6, 7 and 8 semitones.

reveal.text: Matching the major-scale size gives major, and one fewer gives minor.

lead.text: Take the black key between F and G, six semitones above C. Spell it G♭ and the interval from C to it has the letters C D E F G, so it is a fifth, and a perfect fifth would be 7 semitones, so this one is *diminished*. Spell it F♯ and the letters are C D E F, a fourth, and a perfect fourth is 5 semitones, so this one is *augmented*. The sound is the same on a keyboard, but the notation has two names, and the name that is right depends on the spelling in the music.

So semitones alone cannot name an interval. It takes both the letter count, which gives the number, and the semitone count, which gives the quality by comparison with the reference sizes. If you try to name an interval from semitones only, you will sometimes pick the wrong number.

afterFigure.text: The two views are the same keys with two names. In the first the interval is a diminished fifth, and in the second an augmented fourth.

diagram.alt: A keyboard from C4 to C5 with the black key between F and G highlighted and C highlighted. In one view the key is spelled G flat and the interval is a diminished fifth. In the other it is spelled F sharp and the interval is an augmented fourth. Both are 6 semitones.
diagram.caption: Six semitones is one key, but the spelling decides the number. Use the buttons to compare the two names.

reveal.text: The perfect numbers are the unison, fourth, fifth and octave.
Use the table on the earlier screen as a check.

lead.text: If you move the lower note up an octave, the interval turns upside down, and we call the result its **inversion**. The two always fit together to make an octave, so their sizes add up to 12 semitones and their numbers add up to 9: a third becomes a sixth, a fourth a fifth, a second a seventh. The quality flips as well, major to minor and minor to major, augmented to diminished and diminished to augmented, but perfect stays perfect.

An interval larger than an octave is a **compound interval**. We name it by adding 7 to the simple interval's number, since an octave takes 7 off the count of letters. A perfect fifth plus an octave is a perfect twelfth, because 5 + 7 = 12, and its size is 7 + 12 = 19 semitones.

diagram.alt: A bar twelve semitones long, split into two parts. A major third of 4 semitones plus a minor sixth of 8 fills the octave. A perfect fourth of 5 plus a perfect fifth of 7 fills it as well, as does a major second of 2 plus a minor seventh of 10.
diagram.caption: An interval and its inversion always add up to one octave, 12 semitones, and their numbers add to 9. Use the buttons to see three pairs.

steps.headline: Name the interval from A up to F.

workedSteps.text: Count the letters from A up to F, with A as 1. That gives the number.
workedSteps.math: A B C D E F = 6, a sixth

workedSteps.text: Now find the size on the keyboard. A up to F passes A♯, B, C, C♯, D, D♯, E and lands on F.
A major sixth is 9 semitones, which would be A up to F♯. The interval here is one semitone smaller than that.
Name the interval, with its quality and number.

steps.headline: Name the interval from E up to B♭.

workedSteps.text: Count the letters E F G A B. The number is 5.
E up to B would be 7 semitones, a perfect fifth. B♭ is one semitone lower, so E up to B♭ is 6 semitones.
A perfect interval that is a semitone smaller has a particular quality. Name the interval.

reveal.text: Its name is a major tenth, since 3 + 7 = 10.

lessons.orientation: Name an interval by number and quality and find its size in semitones.
lessons.nextAction: Read a key signature and find any key on the circle of fifths.

blocks.text: From C up to G is 7 semitones and from B up to F is 6, yet a musician calls both of them a fifth, because each spans five letter names. The distance between two notes is called an **interval**, and its name comes in two words, such as *minor third* or *perfect fifth*, because a single word can't tell those two fifths apart.
The number counts letter names, and the quality says how big the interval actually is, measured against the major scale.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name an interval from two notes by its number and quality, and say how many semitones it contains.
intro.whyItMatters: Chords, keys and voice leading are all described by their intervals.

recap.keyIdea: An interval's number counts letter names and its quality says which size that number has, so naming one takes both a letter count and a semitone count.

blocks.text: The number comes from counting letters from the lower note to the upper, and the quality compares the size in semitones with the major scale above the lower note. Perfect intervals have no major or minor forms, an interval and its inversion make an octave, and a compound interval is named by adding 7 to the simple number.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses these intervals to read key signatures and the circle of fifths.

lessons.title: Key signatures and the circle of fifths

lead.text: In Lesson 4 we found that G major needs F♯ and D major needs F♯ and C♯. In printed music these are not written beside every F and C. They are collected at the start of each staff, after the clef, in what we call the **key signature**, and every F and C on the staff is then sharp unless a natural cancels it.
The sharps always appear in the same order: **F, C, G, D, A, E, B**, and the flats appear in the reverse order, **B, E, A, D, G, C, F**.

afterFigure.text: The buttons show five keys. Each new sharp is added to those before it, and the order never changes.

diagram.alt: A treble staff with a key signature at the start. In one view there is a sharp on the top line F, giving G major. Other views add sharps or flats in a fixed order: F, C, G, D, A, E, B for sharps and B, E, A, D, G, C, F for flats.
diagram.caption: A key signature puts the sharps or flats of a key at the start of the staff. They always come in the same order. Use the buttons to compare five keys.

reveal.text: The next screen turns this into a rule that works for every key.

lead.text: Reading the key from a signature is quick once you remember where the sharps come from. The last sharp in the list is the **leading tone** of the key, the seventh degree, a semitone below the tonic. So we go up a semitone from the last sharp to find the key. Three sharps, F, C and G, end on G, and a semitone above G is A, so the key is A major. Notice that the last sharp is *not* the key, a slip that is easy to make with a key such as G major, where the last sharp is F.

Flats work another way. The last flat of a signature is the fourth degree of the key, so the key is the *second-to-last* flat. Two flats, B and E, give B♭ major, because the second-to-last flat is B, and four flats, B, E, A and D, give A♭ major. The one exception is F major with a single flat: there is no second-to-last flat, and you just remember it.

afterFigure.text: Each of these rules follows from the sharps and flats being added a fifth apart, which the circle of fifths shows in the next screens.

diagram.alt: Two key signatures with the rule written under each. Three sharps, F C G, end on G, and a semitone above G is A, so A major. Four flats, B E A D, have A as the second-to-last flat, so A flat major.
diagram.caption: Two ways to read a key from its signature. Use the buttons to switch.

reveal.text: The next key along the same pattern, five sharps, ends on A.

lead.text: Why are the sharps in the order F, C, G, D, A, E, B? Each one is a perfect fifth above the one before, F to C, C to G, G to D, and so on, seven semitones each time. The keys follow the same pattern. G is a fifth above C and has one sharp, D is a fifth above G and has two, and each step up a fifth adds the next sharp in the list. Going the other way, down a fifth from C gives F with one flat, then B♭ with two, and each further step down adds the next flat.

Draw the keys round a clock face, C at the top, with a fifth up as each step clockwise, and we get the **circle of fifths**. After twelve steps the circle closes, because twelve fifths of 7 semitones span 84 semitones, which is exactly seven octaves. At the bottom the two directions meet: F♯ major with six sharps and G♭ major with six flats are the same key on the keyboard, spelled in two ways. That is why there are twelve different keys but fifteen key signatures: the seven-sharp key C♯ major and the seven-flat key C♭ major add spellings beyond the overlap.

afterFigure.text: The first view gives the number of sharps or flats for the keys nearest C and for the two spellings at the bottom, and leaves a question mark where you can count the steps yourself. The second picks out A major with three sharps.

diagram.alt: The circle of fifths: C at the top, then G, D, A, E, B and F sharp or G flat clockwise, and D flat, A flat, E flat, B flat and F coming back. The first view gives the sharps or flats of C, G, D, A, F, B flat and the bottom key, with question marks elsewhere. The second marks A major. The third shows the relative minors of C, F and B flat.
diagram.caption: Each step clockwise is a perfect fifth up and adds one sharp. Each step anticlockwise is a perfect fifth down and adds one flat. Use the buttons to see the signatures, one key, and the relative minors.

lead.text: A minor and C major use the very same seven notes and the same signature, with no sharps or flats. They differ in which note is home, and we call A minor the **relative minor** of C major, and C major the relative major of A minor.

To find it, go down a minor third from the major tonic, which is 3 semitones. A is 3 semitones below C, D is 3 below F, and G is 3 below B♭. A single signature therefore names two keys, and which one a piece is in has to be settled from the music itself.

steps.headline: Name the major key that has five flats.

workedSteps.text: Write the flats in order: B, E, A, D, G. There are five, so these are all of them.
With flats, the key is the second-to-last flat. The last flat is G♭, so the key is the flat just before it.
Give the key in words.

steps.headline: Name the major key that has three flats.

workedSteps.text: The flats in order are B, E, A, so the signature has B♭, E♭ and A♭.
Take the second-to-last flat. Give the key in words.

reveal.text: Check: B minor has the same two sharps, F♯ and C♯.

lessons.orientation: Name the major key from a signature, give a key's signature and find its relative minor.
lessons.reviewLabel: Key signatures and the circle of fifths
lessons.nextAction: Build the natural, harmonic and melodic minor scales from their step patterns.

blocks.text: Open a piece of music and, before the first note, you'll see a small cluster of sharps or flats beside the clef. That cluster, the **key signature**, tells a performer which notes to play sharp or flat throughout the piece, and with them which major key it is in. The sharps always appear in the same order, F, C, G, D, A, E, B, and the flats in the reverse order, whatever the piece.
Why that order, and how do we turn a count of sharps or flats into the name of a key?

diagram.alt: A treble staff with the key signature of A major, three sharps on F, C and G.
diagram.caption: Three sharps at the start of a staff mean the piece is in A major, or its relative minor.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name a major key from its signature, give the signature of a key, and find its relative minor.
intro.whyItMatters: Every piece you read has a key signature, and it fixes which notes are sharp or flat.

recap.keyIdea: The sharps and flats of a key signature come in a fixed order, a fifth apart, and that order gives the key from the last sharp or the second-to-last flat.

blocks.text: Each step clockwise round the circle of fifths adds a sharp and each step anticlockwise adds a flat, so counting steps from C gives the signature. The key is a semitone above the last sharp, or the second-to-last flat, and every signature also names a relative minor 3 semitones below the major tonic.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson builds the minor scales from the pattern behind that relative minor.

lessons.title: Minor scales

lead.text: Play the white keys from A up to the next A and you hear a scale with a different character from C major. This is **natural minor**. Its steps are W H W W H W W, so the half steps fall between the second and third degrees and between the fifth and sixth, instead of between the third and fourth and between the seventh and eighth.

It is tempting to describe a minor key as a sad version of a major one. That is a poor description, since the two scales use the same notes and differ in which note is home and in where the half steps fall. The third degree is the clearest difference. It lies 3 semitones above the tonic in minor, a minor third, and 4 above in major, a major third.

diagram.alt: Two keyboards, A natural minor from A4 to A5 using only white keys with the steps W H W W H W W, and C major for comparison with W W H W W W H. The minor scale has its half steps between degrees 2 and 3 and between 5 and 6.
diagram.caption: A natural minor uses the same keys as C major but starts from A, so the half steps fall in different places. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The notes of E natural minor are E, F♯, G, A, B, C, D.
The next screen shows what composers do about this.

lead.text: Without a semitone below the tonic, the scale lacks a leading tone, and the chord built on the dominant doesn't pull strongly toward home. The fix is simple: raise the seventh degree by a semitone. A natural minor with G raised to G♯ gives A, B, C, D, E, F, G♯, A, which we call **harmonic minor**. It is not a new scale to learn from scratch, since it is just natural minor with one note raised.

The raised seventh has a side effect. The sixth degree F and the raised seventh G♯ are now 3 semitones apart, a gap that looks like a second on the staff but is as wide as a minor third. We call it an **augmented second**, and it gives harmonic minor a distinctive sound. D harmonic minor shows it too: D, E, F, G, A, B♭, C♯, D, with 3 semitones between B♭ and C♯.

afterFigure.text: In the second figure the gap marked 3 is the augmented second, the one place where harmonic minor takes a larger step.

reveal.text: The same gap appears in every harmonic minor, between degrees 6 and 7.

lead.text: A melody that has to climb through the augmented second can sound awkward. To smooth it, the **melodic minor** raises the sixth degree too, so that the notes going up step by whole tones and semitones. In A melodic minor going up, the scale is A, B, C, D, E, F♯, G♯, A. Coming down, the leading tone has done its job, and the scale usually returns to natural minor: A, G, F, E, D, C, B, A.
So there are three forms of minor, and they differ only in the sixth and seventh degrees. Natural minor has neither raised, harmonic minor raises the seventh, and ascending melodic minor raises both.

lead.text: The relative minor of C major is A minor, which has the same signature but a tonic 3 semitones lower. The **parallel minor** of C major is C minor, which has the same tonic but a different signature: three flats, B♭, E♭ and A♭. We call two keys with the same tonic **parallel keys**.

To find the signature of a minor key, go up a minor third to its relative major and read the signature of that. C minor's relative major is E♭, which has three flats. Mixing up relative and parallel is a common slip, and the easy way to avoid it is to ask which thing the two keys share.

diagram.alt: Three staves with key signatures. C major has none. A minor, the relative minor, has none either. C minor, the parallel minor, has three flats.
diagram.caption: Relative keys share a signature and have different tonics. Parallel keys share a tonic and have different signatures. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The flats are the same ones that E♭ major has.

workedSteps.text: Start with G natural minor, using the pattern W H W W H W W. Its relative major is B♭, which has two flats.
workedSteps.math: G A B♭ C D E♭ F G

workedSteps.text: Harmonic minor raises the seventh degree by a semitone. The seventh note of G natural minor is F.
Write the scale with the raised note, then name the seventh note.
workedSteps.math: G A B♭ C D E♭ ? G

reveal.text: Check that it is a semitone below E.

lessons.orientation: Build the three minor scales and say how each differs from the major.
lessons.nextAction: Count and notate rhythm in simple and compound metre.

blocks.text: Play the white keys from A up to the next A and listen to the run. It uses exactly the notes of C major, with no sharps or flats, yet it sounds darker and seems to settle somewhere else. Since the notes haven't changed, the difference has to come from where the run starts, and so from where its whole tones and semitones fall.
Where do the steps of a minor scale fall, and why do composers so often alter one or two of its notes when they write a tune in it?

intro.promise: By the end you'll build the natural, harmonic and melodic minor scales and say how each differs from the major.
intro.whyItMatters: Minor keys are half of tonal music, and their chords come from these scales.

recap.keyIdea: Natural minor is W H W W H W W from the tonic, harmonic minor raises its seventh, and ascending melodic minor raises its sixth and seventh.

blocks.text: A minor scale shares its notes with its relative major but starts three semitones lower, so its half steps fall in different places. Raising the seventh gives harmonic minor a leading tone and an augmented second, and raising the sixth as well gives the melodic form going up. A parallel key shares the tonic and not the signature, which is why C minor has three flats and C major none.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from pitch to time, with beats, bars and rhythm.

lessons.title: Rhythm and metre

lead.text: Tap your foot along to a song and you are marking its **beat**, the steady pulse that the notes are organised around. How fast that pulse goes is the **tempo**, and we measure it in beats per minute, abbreviated bpm. Since a minute has 60 seconds, one beat lasts 60 ÷ bpm seconds. At 60 bpm that is one second, at 120 bpm it is half a second, and at 75 bpm it is 60 ÷ 75 = 0.8 seconds.
Beats are grouped into bars of equal length, and a bar of three beats at 75 bpm lasts 3 × 0.8 = 2.4 seconds.

afterFigure.text: Switching tempo changes only the spacing.

diagram.alt: A timeline from 0 to 4 seconds with a dot for each beat. At 60 beats per minute the dots are 1 second apart, at 120 they are 0.5 seconds apart, and at 75 they are 0.8 seconds apart.
diagram.caption: Tempo is how often the beat comes. A faster tempo puts the dots closer together. Use the buttons to compare three tempi.

reveal.text: Each extra beat per minute shortens the beat a little.

lead.text: Written notes tell us how long each sound lasts, relative to the beat. The longest we meet is the **whole note**, which lasts four beats. Halve it and we have the **half note**, with two beats, then the **quarter note**, with one, then the **eighth note**, half a beat, and the **sixteenth note**, a quarter of a beat. The shape changes with the length: the head is open for a whole or half note, filled for shorter ones, a stem is added from the half note, and each flag or beam on the stem halves the length again.
Notice that these lengths are *relative*. This is why we can read a note value without knowing the speed of the piece.

afterFigure.text: The boxes in the figure are all as wide as a bar of four beats. Count how many fit in the bar for each note.

reveal.text: The next screen states the rule for the dot.

lead.text: The dot is a rule about proportion. It adds half of the length of the note it follows, so a dotted half note lasts 2 + 1 = 3 beats, a dotted quarter lasts 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 beats and a dotted eighth lasts 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75 of a beat. It does not add a fixed amount, which is a common slip.

A **tie** is a curved line joining two notes of the same pitch, and it makes them a single sound whose length is the sum of the two. Two beats tied to one more beat gives three, the same as a dotted half note, but a tie can also reach across a barline. A **rest** is a silence, and rests come in the same family of lengths as notes: whole, half, quarter, eighth and so on.

lead.text: Music is divided into **bars**, separated by barlines, and the **time signature** at the start says how each bar is counted. The top number is the number of beats in a bar, and the bottom number names the note value of one beat, with 4 meaning a quarter note, 2 a half note and 8 an eighth note. So 4/4 has four quarter-note beats, and 3/4 has three. The bottom number is not a count: in 3/4 the 4 means *quarter note*, not four beats.

Some metres group the beat in threes. In 6/8 there are six eighth notes in a bar, but they are felt as two beats, each made of three eighths, which is a dotted quarter note. We call a metre where each beat divides into three **compound**, and a metre where it divides into two, like 4/4 or 3/4, **simple**. It is why a waltz in 3/4 and a jig in 6/8, both with six eighth notes' worth of time in the bar, feel different.

afterFigure.text: The coloured boxes in the figure are the beats. In 6/8 there are only two of them, though six notes.

lead.text: In 4/4 the beats are strongest on 1 and 3 and weaker on 2 and 4, and a listener expects new notes to arrive on them. **Syncopation** is what happens when the notes arrive somewhere else, usually on the half-beat between the numbers, which we count as the & of a beat. A tie across a strong beat or a rest on one also does it.

Take the rhythm eighth note, quarter, quarter, quarter, eighth note. The first note starts on 1, but the next three start on the & of 1, the & of 2 and the & of 3. The metre is still being counted, and the notes push against it, which gives the rhythm its lilt.

diagram.alt: A bar of 4/4 divided into eight eighth-note slots numbered 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &. In one view four quarter notes each start on a beat. In the other view the rhythm eighth, quarter, quarter, quarter, eighth has most notes starting on the & between beats, which is syncopation.
diagram.caption: Syncopation puts attacks where the metre does not expect them. Boxes show how long each note lasts, and the warm colour marks notes that start off the beat. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Find how long a bar of 3/4 lasts at 90 beats per minute.

workedSteps.text: Start with the length of one beat. A minute is 60 seconds and there are 90 beats in it.
The top number of the time signature says how many beats are in a bar, which is 3 here.
Multiply the length of a beat by the number of beats, and give the length of the bar in seconds.

reveal.text: Work out the length of a quarter note first.

lessons.orientation: Count note lengths in beats, read a time signature and turn tempo into seconds.
lessons.nextAction: Build triads and seventh chords and name their qualities.

blocks.text: Count 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 at a steady speed and you have the pulse of a waltz, and count 1, 2, 1, 2 at the same speed and you have a march. The notes played over those counts could be identical and the two would still feel completely different, because the beats are grouped differently and the strong beat comes round at a different moment.
How is a pulse like that written down, and how do the lengths of notes relate to it?

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the length of notes in beats, read a time signature, and convert tempo to seconds.
intro.whyItMatters: Rhythm turns a row of notes into music, and every piece you play or read is counted this way.

recap.keyIdea: Tempo gives the length of a beat as 60 divided by the beats per minute, note values halve down from the whole note, and the time signature says how the beats are grouped in a bar.

blocks.text: A dot adds half of a note's own length, a tie adds two notes together, and 6/8 groups six eighths into two beats of three, which is how compound metre differs from 3/4 or 4/4. Syncopation puts the notes between the beats instead of on them, so counting a bar means keeping the beat in mind even when no note falls on it.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson stacks three notes from a scale into chords.

lessons.title: Triads and seventh chords

lead.text: Pick a note from a scale, skip one note, take the next, skip one again, and take the next. From C that gives C, E, G, three notes with a gap of one note between each. We call such a stack of three notes a **triad**, and name its notes by their distance from the lowest, the **root**: the **third** and the **fifth**.
C up to E is 4 semitones, a major third, and E up to G is 3, a minor third. So the triad C E G is a major third with a minor third on top, and it spans 7 semitones from root to fifth.

diagram.alt: The triad C E G shown on a treble staff as three noteheads stacked on adjacent lines or spaces, and on a keyboard with the keys C, E and G highlighted. From C to E is 4 semitones and from E to G is 3.
diagram.caption: A triad is three notes stacked in thirds. On the staff the notes sit on neighbouring lines or neighbouring spaces. Use the buttons to see the same chord on the keyboard.

reveal.text: The next screen sorts triads by the sizes of their two thirds.

lead.text: A third can be a major third of 4 semitones or a minor third of 3, so there are four ways to stack two of them. A **major triad** has a major third below a minor third (4 + 3), a **minor triad** has a minor third below a major third (3 + 4), a **diminished triad** has two minor thirds (3 + 3) and an **augmented triad** has two major thirds (4 + 4). In each case the quality names the interval from root to fifth too: a perfect fifth of 7 for major and minor, a diminished fifth of 6, and an augmented fifth of 8.

On the staff or the keyboard the names do not depend on how the chord sounds. A major chord is *defined* by 4 + 3, and calling it happy is a description of what some listeners feel in some music, which varies with the tune, the tempo and the rest of the harmony. The intervals are what is fixed.

afterFigure.text: The four views build chords on C, so only the third and the fifth change.

diagram.alt: Four boxes pairs showing how a triad on C is built. A major triad is 4 semitones then 3, C E G. A minor triad is 3 then 4, C E flat G. A diminished triad is 3 then 3, C E flat G flat. An augmented triad is 4 then 4, C E G sharp.
diagram.caption: The quality of a triad comes from the two stacked thirds. The number in each box is its size in semitones. Use the buttons to compare the four triads.

reveal.text: Skip a letter each time, and check the sizes of the thirds.

lead.text: Take the notes of C major and build a triad on each, using only those notes. The result is C E G, D F A, E G B, F A C, G B D, A C E and B D F. Their qualities are major, minor, minor, major, major, minor and diminished, and the pattern is the same in every major key, since it comes from the pattern of whole tones and half steps in the scale. We label each triad with a **Roman numeral** for the degree of its root, written in capitals for major (I, IV, V) and small letters for minor (ii, iii, vi) and diminished (vii°).

This is a reliable shortcut. In G major the triad on the sixth degree is E G B, an E minor triad, written vi. Notice that the qualities *alternate* and do not follow the order of the degrees: the triad on the second degree is minor, and the one on the seventh is diminished. The three major chords, I, IV and V, are the main ones of the key, and we use them in the next lesson.

reveal.text: Capitals mark major chords and small letters mark minor ones.
The same two sizes appear in the diminished seventh chords of later courses.

lead.text: A triad can take a fourth note, another third above the fifth, and that gives a **seventh chord**, whose top note is a seventh above the root. The most important one is built on the fifth degree of a major scale. In C major the fifth degree is G, and the triad G B D is major. Add F, a seventh above G, and the chord is G B D F, written **G7** or V7. The seventh F is 10 semitones above G, which makes it a minor seventh.

We call this a **dominant seventh**, since it is built on the dominant, the fifth degree, and it has a major triad with a minor seventh on top. It contains a diminished fifth inside it, between B and F, a tension that wants to move, which is why it so often leads to the tonic chord.

diagram.alt: The dominant seventh chord G7 on a treble staff with the notes G, B, D and F stacked in thirds, and on a ruler of semitones above G, with B at 4, D at 7 and F at 10.
diagram.caption: G7 is a major triad G B D plus a seventh note F, 10 semitones above the root. Use the buttons to see it on the staff and on a ruler.

lead.text: The lowest note of a chord does not decide its name. C, E and G played with C lowest is C major in **root position**, and the same notes with E lowest are still C major, now in **first inversion**. With G lowest it is **second inversion**. The inversion is named by which note of the chord is lowest: the root, the third or the fifth.

Do not confuse this with the inversion of an interval, which flips a third into a sixth. A chord of C E G is a C major triad whatever order they are played in, and the sound changes a little because a different note is at the bottom.

diagram.alt: The notes C, E and G written three ways on a treble staff. In root position C is lowest, in first inversion E is lowest, and in second inversion G is lowest. It is the same chord, C major, each time.
diagram.caption: Moving the lowest note to the top of the chord gives an inversion, and the chord keeps its name. The lowest note is shaded. Use the buttons to compare.

blocks.text: Play three white keys together, C, E and G, and you get a chord that sounds settled and bright. Play D, F and A, and the chord sounds noticeably darker. Both chords are made in the same way, by taking a note, skipping a white key, taking the next, skipping again and taking a third, so the difference can't come from how they were put together.

Why should the same recipe give a different sound? To answer that we need to measure each chord more exactly than by counting white keys, and that measurement names every chord built this way as major, minor, diminished or augmented.

intro.promise: By the end you'll build major, minor, diminished and augmented triads and the dominant seventh, and name the triad on each degree of a major scale.
intro.whyItMatters: Chords are how a tune is accompanied, and progressions are built from these triads.

recap.keyIdea: A triad is two thirds stacked on a root, its quality comes from their sizes, and a major scale gives the pattern major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.

blocks.text: Four stacks of thirds are possible: 4 + 3 is major, 3 + 4 is minor, 3 + 3 is diminished and 4 + 4 is augmented. Roman numerals give the degree and quality of each chord in a key, a minor seventh on top of the major triad on the fifth degree gives the dominant seventh, and inversions change only which note is lowest.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson strings these chords into progressions and cadences.

lessons.title: Progressions and cadences

reveal.text: The next screen explains what that small gap does to a chord.

lead.text: Take G7, the dominant seventh in C major, whose notes are G, B, D and F. Look at B and F in particular. B is the third of the chord and F is the seventh, and they are 6 semitones apart, which is half an octave. We call an interval of 6 semitones a **tritone**, and it sounds unstable: it seems to want to go somewhere, as a clock that stops at ten to twelve seems to want to move.

Where it goes is the nearest notes of the tonic chord. B is the **leading tone** of C major, one semitone below C, and it rises to C. F falls a semitone to E. The two notes move inward, and the pair that was 6 semitones apart is now 4 apart, C and E, which are two notes of the C major triad. That pull is the real reason V goes to I: it is the notes that do the work, and custom only follows from it.

afterFigure.text: The second view shows the two arrows. Neither note has to move far.

diagram.alt: A treble staff with the notes B and F, six semitones apart, taken from the chord G7. A second view shows the two notes resolving inward: B rises by a semitone to C and F falls by a semitone to E, the notes of a C major chord.
diagram.caption: The tritone between B and F is the unstable part of G7. Both notes move by a semitone to the nearest notes of the C chord. Use the buttons to see the resolution.

lead.text: The chords of a key fall into three groups by what they do. The **tonic** group, I and often vi, is home, where the music is at rest. The **predominant** group, ii and IV, leaves home and prepares for what follows. The **dominant** group, V and vii°, creates tension, since both contain the leading tone and want to resolve to I. We call these jobs a chord's **harmonic function**.

Chords tend to move in a chain from tonic to predominant to dominant and back to tonic. A progression such as I, IV, V, I follows this chain exactly, and so does ii, V, I. It can start anywhere in the chain and skip a step, but the dominant almost always goes to the tonic.

diagram.alt: Three boxes in a row: tonic, predominant and dominant, with arrows from tonic to predominant to dominant and one arrow returning from the dominant to the tonic. In C major the tonic box holds C and A minor, the predominant box holds D minor and F, and the dominant box holds G and B diminished. A second view shows the same boxes for G major.
diagram.caption: Chords fall into three jobs. Tonic chords are home, predominant chords leave it, dominant chords create tension, and the usual path returns to the tonic. Use the buttons to see two keys.

reveal.text: The V chord of G major shares the notes F♯ and A with the key.

lead.text: The chords at the end of a phrase act like punctuation, and we call such a closing pair a **cadence**. The strongest is the **authentic cadence**, V to I, which settles on the tonic after the tension of V. The **half cadence** ends on V itself, so the phrase stops and waits, like a comma. The **plagal cadence**, IV to I, closes more softly. The **deceptive cadence** goes from V to vi, and it is named so because the ear expects I and gets the submediant, a chord that shares two notes with I but is not home.

So a cadence is named by the chords it contains, taken from the last two. Notice that V to vi is not a mistake in the harmony. It is a deliberate surprise, and a composer uses it to extend the phrase.

afterFigure.text: In C major the pairs are G to C, any chord to G, F to C and G to A minor.

diagram.alt: Four cadences shown as pairs of chords in C major. The authentic cadence is V to I, G to C. The half cadence ends on V, for example C to G. The plagal cadence is IV to I, F to C. The deceptive cadence is V to vi, G to A minor.
diagram.caption: A cadence is the pair of chords that closes a phrase, and it is named by what the pair does. Use the buttons to see the four.

reveal.text: The substitute chord shares two notes with I.
A half cadence can follow I, ii or IV.

lead.text: The numerals are keyless: I V vi IV in G major is G, D, Em, C, and in C major it is C, G, Am, F. To write a progression in a key, list the notes of the major scale, find the degree for each numeral, and add its quality, which a capital numeral gives as major and a small one as minor.
A singer who finds a tune too high can shift every chord by the same step, and the numerals stay exactly as they were.

afterFigure.text: Look down a column and the numeral stays while the chord name changes.

diagram.alt: Two tables of chord progressions in the keys of C, G, D and A. The progression I V vi IV gives C G Am F in C major, G D Em C in G major, D A Bm G in D major and A E F sharp minor D in A major. The progression I IV V I gives C F G C, G C D G, D G A D and A D E A.

steps.headline: Write the progression I V vi IV in E major.

workedSteps.text: Write the notes of E major and number them.
workedSteps.math: E F♯ G♯ A B C♯ D♯

workedSteps.text: The I chord is built on the first degree, E, and it is major. The V chord is on B, with D♯ and F♯, and it is major.
The vi chord is built on the sixth degree, C♯, with E and G♯. Name it, with its quality.
The IV chord is built on the fourth degree, A, and is major.

reveal.text: Check that the chord is minor, as vi always is.

lessons.orientation: Explain chord function, name the cadences and write a progression in any major key.
lessons.nextAction: Spot parallel fifths and octaves and fix them in four-part writing.

blocks.text: Play the chord G7 on a piano, G, B, D and F together, and then the chord C, E, G, and the second chord sounds like an arrival. Stop on the G7 instead and the music hangs in the air, as if waiting for the C chord to come. That pull from one chord to the next ends a great many hymns and songs, and it can be traced to particular notes in the first chord.

Which notes pull, where do they go, and how do composers use the pull to shape music? Following those notes explains why some chords sound like home and others like a step away from it, and it gives us names for the four standard ways a phrase can end, which we can then find and write in any major key.

diagram.alt: A treble staff with the notes B and F from the chord G7, six semitones apart, and then moving to C and E.
diagram.caption: The two unstable notes of G7 move a semitone each to settle on the notes of C.

intro.promise: By the end you'll explain tonic, predominant and dominant function, name the four standard cadences and write a progression in any major key.
intro.whyItMatters: Songs are built on a few chord progressions, and recognising them lets you play and write music faster.

recap.keyIdea: Chords act as tonic, predominant or dominant, and V pulls to I because the tritone of V7 and the leading tone each resolve by a semitone.

blocks.text: Four cadences end phrases: the authentic V to I, the half cadence on V, the plagal IV to I and the deceptive V to vi. Roman numerals give the progression without a key, and replacing each numeral with the chord on that degree writes it in any key.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how voices move from one chord to the next.

lessons.title: Voice leading

lead.text: A chord on the page is a vertical thing, but a choir sings it as four separate lines, one for each voice: **soprano**, **alto**, **tenor** and **bass**. Each voice has a range of roughly an octave and a half, the soprano around C4 to G5, the alto G3 to D5, the tenor C3 to G4 and the bass E2 to C4.

The idea of **voice leading** is that each of those lines should be worth singing in its own right, moving smoothly, and that together they should make sense. Bach's chorales are the standard demonstration.

diagram.caption: Each voice covers about an octave and a half, and neighbouring voices overlap. Use the buttons to see the ranges and one chord.
