reveal.text: The next screen classifies how the two voices can move.

lead.text: Take two voices and follow each from one chord to the next. If they move in the same direction and keep the same interval, the motion is **parallel**. If they move in the same direction by different amounts, so the interval changes, it is **similar**. If one voice holds its note while the other moves, it is **oblique**. If one rises while the other falls, it is **contrary**.
The four are not equally independent. Contrary and oblique motion give the lines the most freedom, since the voices go their own ways, while parallel motion makes one voice a shadow of the other.

afterFigure.text: Use the buttons to see each.

diagram.alt: A treble staff with two voices, each moving from one note to the next. In parallel motion both rise and keep the same interval. In similar motion both rise by different amounts. In oblique motion one voice holds while the other moves. In contrary motion one rises and the other falls.
diagram.caption: Two voices can move in four ways. Use the buttons to see each one.

reveal.text: Similar motion is when both move the same way.

lead.text: A perfect fifth or an octave is a very pure interval, and the two notes blend almost into one. If two voices sit a fifth apart and both rise by a step, the ear hears the new pair of notes as the same blend moved up, and the two voices lose their separate identities. We call this **parallel fifths**, and the same thing with an octave is **parallel octaves**. In the common-practice style, the tonal harmony of roughly 1650 to 1900 that Bach's chorales are used to teach, both are avoided.

The rule is narrower than it sounds. It does not say that fifths are bad, since a fifth between two voices is fine. It forbids *moving* from one perfect fifth to another in the same direction, or from one octave to another. The usual fix is to make one of the voices move the other way, so the motion becomes contrary and the interval changes. Bass C3 to D3 with tenor G3 to A3 gives parallel fifths, and the tenor falling to F3 repairs it.

afterFigure.text: The first view shows the fault, and the second shows the repair.

diagram.alt: A bass staff showing a bass voice moving C3 to D3 and a tenor voice moving G3 to A3, both rising, so the fifth C to G moves to the fifth D to A. In the second view the tenor falls from G3 to F3 instead, which avoids the parallel fifths.
diagram.caption: Two voices a fifth apart that rise together by the same step make parallel fifths. Moving one of them the other way fixes it. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Check the direction of both voices as well.

lead.text: Where two chords share a note, keep it in the same voice, because a voice that holds moves no distance. The other voices move by the smallest steps available, which keeps the joins smooth. The bass often moves differently, by leap, since it gives the progression its foundation and keeps it independent of the upper voices.

The leading tone has one more duty. In V7 to I the leading tone, B in C major, rises to C, and the seventh of the chord, F, falls to E, as in the last lesson. Writing every voice by the nearest note is smooth but can produce parallels, so each join has to be checked for them.

diagram.alt: Two chords written on a grand staff with each of the four voices a different colour and a line joining each voice to its next note. G7 resolves to C: the soprano falls from D to C, the alto from F to E, the tenor rises from B to C, and the bass leaps from G to C.
diagram.caption: In V7 to I the leading tone B rises to C and the seventh F falls to E, while the bass leaps. Use the buttons to compare it with I to IV, where one voice keeps its note.

steps.headline: Fix parallel fifths in a move from C major to D minor, where the bass goes C3 to D3 and the tenor G3 to A3.

workedSteps.text: First measure the interval between the voices. C3 to G3 is 7 semitones, a perfect fifth, and D3 to A3 is also 7.
Both voices rise, so this is parallel fifths. The chord D minor is D, F and A, so the tenor may take F instead of A.
Now the tenor falls while the bass rises, which is contrary motion. Count the semitones between D3 and F3.

steps.headline: Check the join from C major to F major in which the bass goes C3 to F3 and the tenor G3 to A3.

workedSteps.text: Before the move C3 and G3 are a perfect fifth, 7 semitones apart. Both voices rise, so we must see whether they land on a perfect interval.
After the move the bass is on F3 and the tenor is on A3. Count the semitones between them.
That is a major third, not a perfect interval, so these two voices make no parallel fifths.

reveal.text: The seventh of V7, C, falls to B.

lessons.orientation: Join two chords without parallel fifths or octaves and name the motion between two voices.
lessons.nextAction: Describe a piece's form from its phrases and sections, and count a 12-bar blues.

blocks.text: Sing the soprano line of a hymn by itself and it makes a tune. Sing the bass by itself and it makes one too, and so do the alto and the tenor, so a four-part chorale is really four tunes sung at once, each moving from its note in one chord to its note in the next. The way each of those lines moves is called **voice leading**.
What are the ways two lines can move against each other, and which of them does a composer avoid?

diagram.alt: Four voices on a grand staff, each in a different colour, with a line joining each note to the next as a chord of G7 resolves to C.
diagram.caption: Each coloured line is one voice. The lines move by small steps, and only the bass leaps.

intro.promise: By the end you'll join two chords in four voices without parallel fifths or octaves, and name the motion between two voices.
intro.whyItMatters: Voice leading is what makes chord progressions sound like music and not like blocks.

recap.keyIdea: Voices move in parallel, similar, oblique or contrary motion, and moving in parallel from one perfect fifth or octave to another is avoided.

blocks.text: To join two chords smoothly, keep the notes the chords share, move the other voices by small steps and let the bass move independently, then check every pair of voices for parallel fifths and octaves. The leading tone rises to the tonic and the seventh of V7 falls, and when parallels appear the usual repair is to send one voice the other way.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson steps back from single joins to the layout of whole phrases and pieces.

lessons.title: Phrase and form

lead.text: Sing a familiar tune and you will find it breathes in places, where a thought comes to rest. A stretch of music from one such resting place to the next is a **phrase**, and it is most often four bars long. What makes the resting place is a cadence, the chord pair we met in the last lesson, so that a phrase is, in effect, a progression with its punctuation attached.

Two phrases often pair as a question and an answer, which we call a **period**. The first, the **antecedent**, ends on a weaker cadence, usually a half cadence on V that leaves the harmony open. The second, the **consequent**, covers the same ground but ends on a stronger one, an authentic cadence on I.

diagram.alt: Eight bars of chords in two groups of four. In C major the antecedent phrase is C, A minor, F, G and ends on V with a half cadence. The consequent phrase is C, F, G, C and ends on I with an authentic cadence. A second view shows the same period in G major.
diagram.caption: A period is two phrases. The first leaves the harmony open and the second closes it. Use the buttons to see the period in two keys.

lead.text: Larger pieces are built from sections, and we label each section with a capital letter, giving the same letter whenever the same music returns. **Binary form** has two sections, AB. **Ternary form** is ABA, a statement, a contrast and a return. A **rondo** is ABACA, in which the main theme A comes back after each contrasting section, so it is heard three times. Many modern songs use **verse-chorus** form, in which a verse and a chorus alternate, often with a bridge before the last chorus.
Notice that form is not the same as style. It describes how sections are arranged and repeated, and a pop song and a Baroque dance can both be binary.

afterFigure.text: Use the buttons to look at four layouts. The returning colour is the returning music.

diagram.alt: Block diagrams of four layouts. Binary form has two sections, A and B. Ternary form is A, B, A. Rondo is A, B, A, C, A, with A returning three times. A verse-chorus layout alternates verse and chorus, with a bridge before the last chorus.
diagram.caption: Form is the layout of sections, and each letter stands for a section. A repeated letter is a return of the same music. Use the buttons to see four layouts.

The next screen sets out which chord goes in which bar.

lead.text: The **twelve-bar blues** is one of the most common chord patterns in popular music. It uses only the I, IV and V chords of a key, laid out in three rows of four bars. In C it runs C, C, C, C in the first row, F, F, C, C in the second and G, F, C, C in the third. So there are four bars of I, then two of IV and two of I, then V, IV and two of I, and the last two bars sometimes end with V so that the pattern goes round again. One time through all twelve bars is called a **chorus**.

The pattern is the same in every key, with the numerals fixed. In G the second row starts on C and the third on D. Counting by bars and counting by beats give different numbers. A twelve-bar blues in 4/4 is 12 bars but 48 beats, and at 96 beats per minute each bar lasts 2.5 seconds, so one chorus lasts 30 seconds.

afterFigure.text: Notice that bar 9 is the only place the V chord is heard in the main pattern.

diagram.alt: Twelve boxes in three rows of four bars each, showing the chord of each bar. In C the first row is C, C, C, C, the second F, F, C, C, and the third G, F, C, C. In G the chords are G, G, G, G, then C, C, G, G, then D, C, G, G.

lead.text: Sonata form is the layout of the opening movement of many classical sonatas and symphonies, and it applies the idea of key to a whole piece. The **exposition** presents two themes, the first in the home key and the second in a new key, usually the dominant in a major-key piece. The **development** takes the themes apart and sends them through many keys. The **recapitulation** brings both themes back.

The point is that the second theme, which was in a new key in the exposition, now returns in the home key, so the key conflict created at the beginning is settled by the end. In a piece in F major, the second theme is in C in the exposition and in F in the recapitulation.

diagram.alt: Sonata form drawn as three blocks: an exposition that presents two themes, a development that transforms them, and a recapitulation that brings both back. A second view shows keys for a piece in F major: the exposition has theme 1 in F and theme 2 in C, and the recapitulation has both themes in F.
diagram.caption: In sonata form the second theme is in a new key at first and comes home at the end. Use the buttons to compare the layout and the keys.

steps.headline: Find how long one chorus of a twelve-bar blues in 4/4 lasts at 120 beats per minute.

workedSteps.text: Start with the number of beats in one chorus. There are 12 bars and each bar of 4/4 has 4 beats.
At 120 beats per minute, one beat lasts 60 divided by 120 seconds.
Multiply the beats by the length of a beat, and give the length of one chorus in seconds.

reveal.text: The IV chord of G major is C.
The A section is heard three times.

lessons.orientation: Describe a piece's form from its phrases and sections, and count a twelve-bar blues.
lessons.nextAction: You can now read notes and keys, name intervals and chords, count rhythm, and describe how a piece is built.

blocks.text: A great many songs follow the same plan: a verse, then a chorus, then a second verse to new words, then the chorus again. If we write each section as a letter, using a new letter for new music and the same letter whenever music returns, that plan becomes A B A B, and we've described the song's **form** without naming a single note.
Form works at every scale, from a phrase of four bars to the whole of a symphony. What are its building blocks, and what layouts do composers make from them?

diagram.alt: Block diagrams of a binary and a ternary layout, with each section a coloured block and a letter.
diagram.caption: Each letter is a section and the same letter means the same music.

intro.promise: By the end you'll describe a piece's form from its phrases and sections, and count the length of a twelve-bar blues.
intro.whyItMatters: Hearing form tells you where you are in a piece and what is about to happen.

recap.keyIdea: A phrase ends at a cadence, two phrases make a period, sections are named by letters, and the twelve-bar blues and sonata form are larger layouts built from the same ideas.

blocks.text: A period pairs an antecedent on a half cadence with a consequent on an authentic one, and a piece can be binary, ternary, a rondo or verse-chorus depending on how its sections return. The twelve-bar blues is I, IV and V in three rows of four bars, and sonata form brings the second theme home to the main key in the recapitulation.

questions.prompt: The A key near the middle of a piano vibrates 440 times a second. The next A up the keyboard has the same letter and sounds like the same note, only higher. Roughly how fast do you expect it to vibrate?
hints: Same letter name suggests a fixed relationship between the two frequencies.
Think of a relationship that repeats every time you climb to the next A.
The relationship is a multiplication by a fixed amount, and the amount is a small whole number.

acceptedIdeas: About twice as fast, about 880 times a second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About twice as fast, about 880 times a second

questions.onCorrect: Every A on a piano has twice the frequency of the A below it, which is why they share a name.

misconceptions.feedback: A rise of 10 Hz is a very small step, much smaller than the distance from one A to the next. The next A is a fixed multiple of 440.
660 Hz is 440 plus half of 440, and it is close to the E that lies between the two As, a note with a different name. The next A is a larger multiple of 440.
Ten times 440 is more than three octaves up. The next A is the nearest key above that sounds like the same note, so the multiple is much smaller.

choices.label: About half as fast again, about 660 times a second
A little faster, about 450 times a second
About ten times as fast, about 4,400 times a second
About twice as fast, about 880 times a second

questions.prompt: G3 vibrates at 196 Hz. What is the frequency in Hz of the G one octave below G3, which is G2?
hints: Going up an octave doubles the frequency.
Going down is the reverse of going up.
Halve 196.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An octave down halves the frequency: 196 ÷ 2 = 98 Hz.

questions.onCorrect: Halving works the same way for every note, so G1, another octave down, is 49 Hz.

misconceptions.feedback: Subtracting 196 would leave nothing. Going down an octave halves the frequency.
That is G4, the G above G3. Going down is the reverse.

questions.prompt: Starting on one C of the keyboard and counting each step to the nearest key above, black or white, how many steps does it take to land on the next C?
hints: Count every key, black and white, not only the white ones.
White keys: C D E F G A B give 7 steps up to the next C; add the black keys between.
There are 5 black keys in the octave, and 7 + 5 is the total.
questions.onCorrect: Twelve steps is one octave, whatever key it starts on.

misconceptions.feedback: Eight is the number of letter names from C to the next C, counting both ends. The keyboard also has black keys, and every key is a step.
That counts only the white keys. The black keys are keys too, and each is a step.
Thirteen is the number of keys from one C to the next with both Cs included. A step is the move from one key to the next, so the first C is where the counting starts.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are there from D4 up to A4?
hints: Count every key you pass, black and white, ending on A.
D to E is 2, E to F is 1, F to G is 2, and G to A is 2.
Add the four distances together.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From D to A the steps pass D♯, E, F, F♯, G, G♯ and reach A: seven steps.

questions.onCorrect: Seven semitones is the span that a later lesson calls a perfect fifth.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the letters D E F G A. The black keys also count as steps.
That counts only the white-key letters between D and A, leaving out both ends and the black keys.

questions.prompt: What do we call the distance from one key to the nearest key above or below it, whether black or white?
hints: The word has a number-like prefix meaning half.
Twelve of these make an octave.
questions.onCorrect: The same step is called a half step in American usage, and a whole tone is two semitones.

questions.prompt: E4 is 5 semitones below A4. Using 440 × 2^(n/12) with n = −5, what is the frequency of E4 in Hz, to the nearest 0.1 Hz?
hints: Each semitone down divides the frequency by 2^(1/12), so 5 of them divide by 2^(5/12).
Work out 2^(−5/12) on a calculator first, then multiply by 440.
questions.onCorrect: E4 is the E just above middle C, and 329.63 Hz is its equal-tempered frequency.

misconceptions.feedback: 466.2 Hz is the A♯ one semitone above A4. E4 lies five semitones below A4, so the exponent is negative.
That is a full octave down. Five semitones is less than that.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are there from F3 up to B3?
hints: Count every key you pass, black and white, ending on B.
There is a black key above F, G and A, but none between E and F.
Steps from F: F♯, G, G♯, A, A♯, B.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F to B passes F♯, G, G♯, A and A♯ and lands on B: six steps. This distance is the only one between white keys of a letter apart that is neither 5 nor 7.

questions.onCorrect: F up to B is the one fourth on the white keys that is a semitone wider than the others.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the letters F G A B, which leaves out the black keys.
Five semitones is F up to the B♭ below B. Count one more step.

questions.prompt: G4 vibrates at about 392 Hz. What is the frequency in Hz of the next G above it, G5?
hints: Each octave up multiplies the frequency by the same amount.
That amount is the same one that took 440 to 880.
Double 392.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One octave up doubles the frequency: 2 × 392 = 784 Hz.

questions.onCorrect: The Gs from G2 to G5 run 98, 196, 392 and 784 Hz, each twice the last, just as the As do.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds half of 392. Going up an octave doubles the frequency.
That adds 440, the step from A4 to A5. An octave is a doubling, not an addition.

questions.prompt: Which pair of frequencies is exactly one octave apart?
hints: An octave is a ratio, not a gap in hertz.
Divide the higher frequency by the lower one.
questions.onCorrect: Pairs at 200 and 400, or 400 and 800, all sound the same note in a different register.

misconceptions.feedback: 300 is 1.5 times 200, the ratio of a fifth. An octave is a ratio of 2.
250 is 1.25 times 200. An octave is a ratio of 2.
1600 is 8 times 200, which is three octaves.

questions.prompt: A note sits on the third line from the bottom of the treble staff. Give its letter name and octave, for example C4.
hints: Lines of the treble staff from the bottom: E, G, B, D, F.
The treble clef circles the G line, the second line, which is G4. Count up one line.
questions.onCorrect: B4 is the line above G4, and it sits at the centre of the staff.

questions.prompt: Imagine the bass staff drawn directly below the treble staff. The top line of the bass staff is A3 and the bottom line of the treble staff is E4. How many letter names lie strictly between those two notes?
hints: Write the letters upward from A, ending when you reach E.
Remember that after G the letters start again at A, and a new octave number begins at C.
Do not count A3 or E4 themselves.
questions.onCorrect: The middle one of the three, C4, is middle C, which is why it has to be written on a ledger line in both staves.

misconceptions.feedback: The letters run A, B, C, D, E, so going up from A3 to E4 we pass B3, C4 and D4 on the way.
An octave above A3 is A4, which is higher than E4. The two lines are much closer than that, with only B3, C4 and D4 between them.
Two octaves above A3 is A5, far above the treble staff's bottom line. Only B3, C4 and D4 lie between A3 and E4.

choices.label: None, because E4 comes straight after A3

questions.prompt: A note sits on the first ledger line below the bass staff. Give its name and octave.
hints: The bottom line of the bass staff is G2.
Below G2 comes the space F2, and then the ledger line.
questions.onCorrect: Counting away from the staff works the same way below it as above it, one letter for each line or space.

questions.prompt: In the treble clef, a note sits in the fourth space from the bottom. Give its letter name and octave, counting up from the G line.
hints: Start on the G line (G4) and move up one line or space at a time.
G4, then the space A4, the line B4, the space C5, the line D5, then the fourth space.
questions.onCorrect: The fourth space is E5, the top space of the treble staff, found by counting five steps up from G4.

questions.prompt: In the bass clef, a note sits in the second space from the bottom. Give its letter name and octave, counting down from the F line.
hints: The bass clef's two dots surround the fourth line, which is F3.
Counting down from F3: space E3, line D3, then the second space.
questions.onCorrect: Counting down three steps from F3 gives E3, D3 and then C3.

questions.prompt: A note sits on the second ledger line below the treble staff. Give its letter name and octave.
hints: The bottom line of the treble staff is E4, and the first ledger line below it is C4.
From C4 go down one more step to the space and one more to the second ledger line.
questions.onCorrect: The ledger lines count away from the staff, so the second one below the treble staff is A3, with B3 in the space between.

questions.prompt: A note sits on the top line of the treble staff. Give its letter name and octave.
hints: Treble lines from the bottom: E4, G4, B4, D5 and one more.
Count the lines up to the fifth.
questions.onCorrect: F5 is the highest line of the treble staff, and the space just below it is E5.

questions.prompt: A note sits in the top space of the bass staff, between the fourth and fifth lines. Which note is it?
hints: The bass staff lines are G2, B2, D3, F3, A3.
The top space lies between F3 and A3.
questions.onCorrect: G3 is the top space of the bass staff, between F3 and A3.

misconceptions.feedback: F3 is the fourth line itself, the line the clef's dots surround. The space above it is the next letter.
A3 is the top line. The space below it, between the fourth and fifth lines, is one letter lower.
B3 lies above the top line, outside the staff.

questions.prompt: The treble clef is also called the clef of which letter?
hints: The clef curls round one line of the staff.
That line is the second from the bottom, and it is G4.
questions.onCorrect: The curl of the treble clef circles the G line, and an older name for the clef is the G clef.

questions.prompt: Counting every key, black and white, how many semitones are there from E up to B?
hints: Count each key you pass, ending on B.
E to F is already a semitone, since no black key sits between them.
The keys after E are F, F♯, G, G♯, A, A♯, B.
questions.onCorrect: E to B is the same distance as D to A, so the span of seven semitones turns up on many different white-key pairs.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the letters E F G A B. The black keys are keys as well, and each is a step.
That is one too few. E and F touch, so E to F is a single step, and from F there are black keys between each white key up to B.
Eight would mean a black key between every pair of white keys. E and F touch, so the first step from E is only a semitone, and the total is one less.

questions.prompt: A note is written on the second line of the treble staff with a flat sign before it. Give its name in words, for example A sharp.
hints: The second line of the treble staff is G4.
A flat lowers a note by one semitone.
questions.onCorrect: G♭ is one semitone below G, and it is the same key as F♯.

questions.prompt: Which note names the same key as D♯?
hints: A sharp raises the note by a semitone. Which key is that above D?
Two names for one key: one counts up from a lower letter, one counts down from a higher letter.
questions.onCorrect: D♯ is named from the D below it and E♭ from the E above it, and both name the same black key.

misconceptions.feedback: D♭ is one semitone below D, while D♯ is one semitone above it, so they are two keys apart.
E♯ is the key one semitone above E, which is the white key F.
C♯ is a semitone below D, and D♯ is a semitone above it.

questions.prompt: F♭ is the same key as which white key? Give its letter.
hints: F♭ is one semitone below F.
No black key sits between E and F.
questions.onCorrect: Because E and F touch, lowering F by a semitone lands on E, a white key.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are there from F♯ up to C?
hints: Start at F♯ and count each key above it.
Remember that B to C is a single semitone.
The keys above F♯ are G, G♯, A, A♯, B, C.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Counting upward from F♯: G is 1, G♯ is 2, A is 3, A♯ is 4, B is 5 and C is 6.

questions.onCorrect: F♯ to C is the distance known as a tritone, six semitones, which is half an octave.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops one key early. Count up to C itself, and recall that B and C touch.
That counts one too many. Start counting from the key after F♯.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are there from B♭ up to F?
hints: Start counting from the key above B♭, which is B.
B to C is a single semitone, and so is E to F.
The keys above B♭ are B, C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From B♭: B is 1, C is 2, C♯ is 3, D is 4, D♯ is 5, E is 6 and F is 7.

questions.onCorrect: B♭ to F is seven semitones, the same size as E to B.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts letters, B C D E F. Count every key.
That is one short. Count from the key above B♭ up to and including F.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are there from E♯ up to A?
hints: Find which key E♯ names.
E♯ is the same key as F.
Count from F up to A.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: E♯ is the same key as F, so the count runs F♯ 1, G 2, G♯ 3, A 4.

questions.onCorrect: Spelling does not change the key, so E♯ to A is the same as F to A.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats E♯ as if it were E. E♯ is the key above E.
That counts the keys between E♯ and A and leaves out A itself.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are there from A♭ up to D?
hints: A♭ is a black key, so the first step goes to the white key A.
B to C is a single semitone.
The keys above A♭ are A, B♭, B, C, C♯, D.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From A♭: A is 1, B♭ is 2, B is 3, C is 4, C♯ is 5 and D is 6.

questions.onCorrect: A♭ to D is six semitones, half an octave.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one short. Count every key from A♭ up to D.
That is one too many. The first key above A♭ is A.

questions.prompt: Give another name for G♯, the black key one semitone above G, in words, for example C sharp.
hints: The same black key can be named from the letter above it.
Which white key sits just above G, and which way do you count from it?
questions.onCorrect: A♭ and G♯ name the same key, and which one is used depends on the key of the music.

questions.prompt: Which pair of names refers to the same key on the keyboard?
hints: Work out which key each name points to, then compare.
Think about which letters have no black key between them.
questions.onCorrect: E♯ is F, because E and F are a semitone apart and the sharp moves E up by exactly that.

misconceptions.feedback: B♯ is the key above B, which is C, so it is not B.
F♭ is one semitone below F, which is E, while F♯ is one above F.
A♭ is one semitone below A and A♯ is one above it, so they are two semitones apart.

questions.prompt: Start on G and apply the steps whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. What is the seventh note? Give it in words, for example C sharp.
hints: The scale begins G, A, B, C, D, E.
From E, a whole tone is two semitones. Is that step to F or to a black key?
questions.onCorrect: G major needs an F♯, because the step from E to F is only a semitone, but the pattern asks for a whole tone there.

misconceptions.feedback: E to F is only a semitone, but the sixth step of the pattern asks for a whole tone, so the seventh note has to be the black key above F.
E is the sixth note, a whole tone above D. The seventh note comes one more whole tone above E.
G sharp is two whole tones above E. One whole tone above E lands on the black key just above F.

questions.prompt: What is the fourth note of B major? Give its letter.
hints: B major's first three notes are B, C♯, D♯.
The step from the third to the fourth note is a half step.
questions.onCorrect: D♯ to E is a semitone, so the fourth note of B major is E, a white key.

questions.prompt: In any major scale, how many semitones are there from the tonic up to the fourth note?
hints: Write the pattern under the degrees and take the steps from degree 1 to degree 4.
Those are the first three steps of W W H W W W H.
Add their sizes in semitones.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first three steps of the pattern are W W H, so the tonic to the fourth note is 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 semitones.

questions.onCorrect: The fourth degree is the subdominant, and 5 semitones is the size of the interval a later lesson calls a perfect fourth.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops at the third degree, two whole tones up. The step from the third to the fourth adds one more semitone.
That treats every step as a whole tone. The third step of the pattern is a half step.

questions.prompt: Build A major with the pattern W W H W W W H. What is its seventh note? Give it in words, for example C sharp.
hints: The scale so far is A, B, C♯, D, E, F♯.
The seventh note is a whole tone above F♯.
questions.onCorrect: G♯ is a semitone below A, which is the half step that closes the scale.

questions.prompt: Build F major with the pattern. What is the fourth note, written so that each letter name is used once? Give it in words, for example C sharp.
hints: F major begins F, G, A. The fourth letter is B.
The step from A to B is a whole tone, but the pattern asks for a half step here.
questions.onCorrect: A to the key above it is a semitone, which is B♭. Writing it as A♯ would use the letter A twice.

questions.prompt: What is the leading tone of A♭ major, the note a semitone below the tonic? Give it in words, for example C sharp.
hints: The leading tone is the seventh degree.
A♭ major is A♭, B♭, C, D♭, E♭, F and then the seventh note.
questions.onCorrect: G lies a semitone below A♭ and pulls upward to it, a white key even though the tonic is a black one.

questions.prompt: What is the seventh note of E♭ major? Give it in words, for example G sharp.
hints: E♭ major begins E♭, F, G, A♭, B♭, C.
The seventh note is a whole tone above C.
questions.onCorrect: D is a semitone below E♭, which is the half step that closes the scale.

questions.prompt: What is the sixth note of B♭ major? Give its letter.
hints: B♭ major begins B♭, C, D, E♭, F.
The step from F to the sixth note is a whole tone.
questions.onCorrect: F to G is a whole tone, so the sixth degree of B♭ major is the white key G.

questions.prompt: In any major scale, how many semitones are there from the tonic up to the dominant, the fifth note?
hints: Add up the steps from degree 1 to degree 5.
That is the first four steps of the pattern: W, W, H, W.
A whole tone is 2 and a half step is 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first four steps of W W H W W W H are 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 7 semitones, so the dominant is 7 semitones above the tonic.

questions.onCorrect: Seven semitones is a perfect fifth, and the dominant is always that far above the tonic.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds five steps. Degree 5 is reached after four steps.
Check each step: a whole tone is 2 semitones, not 1.5.

questions.prompt: C up to E is a third of 4 semitones, and D up to F is also a third. How does the size of D up to F compare?
hints: Count each key from D up to F, black and white.
E and F touch on the keyboard.
The keys above D are D♯, E, F.
questions.onCorrect: A third can be 3 or 4 semitones, so the number alone does not give the size.

misconceptions.feedback: 4 semitones is the size of C up to E. The step from E to F is only a semitone, which makes D up to F smaller.
Both thirds skip one white key, but between D and F the keys E and F touch, so D up to F has fewer semitones, not more.
2 semitones is a whole tone, from D to E. F lies one semitone further on.

choices.label: The same, 4 semitones, since both are thirds

questions.prompt: Name the interval from D up to F♯, with its quality and number, for example minor sixth.
hints: Count the letters D, E, F: the number is 3.
D to F♯ is 4 semitones, and the size of this number in the major scale is 4.
questions.onCorrect: D up to F♯ matches the third degree of D major, so it is a major third.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are there in a major sixth?
hints: Use the sixth note of a major scale, counted from the tonic.
Add the steps W W H W W.
A whole tone is 2 and a half step is 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A major sixth is the sixth degree of a major scale, and counting W W H W W gives 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 9 semitones.

questions.onCorrect: A major sixth is 9 semitones, and a minor sixth is one fewer, 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a minor sixth. A major sixth is the size found in the major scale, one semitone larger.
That is a perfect fifth. The sixth reaches one letter higher.

questions.prompt: What does a minor third become when it is inverted? Give its quality and number.
hints: The numbers add up to 9: 9 − 3 gives the new number.
Inverting swaps major and minor.
The sizes add up to 12: 3 + 9.
questions.onCorrect: A minor third of 3 semitones fits with a major sixth of 9 to make an octave of 12.

questions.prompt: Name the interval from A up to F, with its quality and number.
hints: Count the letters A B C D E F, then count the semitones from A to F.
The major sixth above A is F♯, which is 9 semitones.
questions.onCorrect: A to F is 8 semitones, one fewer than the major sixth, so it is a minor sixth.

questions.prompt: Name the interval from E up to B♭, with its quality and number.
hints: Count the letters E F G A B: the number is 5.
E to B♭ is one semitone less than the perfect fifth E to B.
questions.onCorrect: E to B♭ is 6 semitones and has 5 letter names, so it is a diminished fifth.

questions.prompt: C4 up to E5 is a major third plus an octave. How many semitones is that?
hints: Split the interval into an octave and a simple interval.
A major third is 4 semitones.
Add 12 to the size of the simple interval.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An octave is 12 semitones and a major third is 4, so the compound interval is 12 + 4 = 16 semitones.

questions.onCorrect: The interval from C4 to E5 is called a major tenth: its number is 3 + 7 = 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the simple third alone. The octave adds 12 more.
That is a minor tenth, 12 + 3. C up to E is a major third, 4 semitones.

questions.prompt: Which of these names does not belong to any interval?
hints: Which numbers have major and minor forms, and which are perfect?
The perfect numbers are the unison, fourth, fifth and octave.
questions.onCorrect: Fourths can be perfect, augmented or diminished, but never major or minor.

misconceptions.feedback: Thirds come in major and minor forms, so this name exists.
The fifth is a perfect interval, so this name exists.
Sixths come in major and minor forms, so this name exists.

questions.prompt: How many semitones are there in a minor seventh?
hints: The major seventh above the tonic is 11 semitones.
Minor is one semitone smaller than major.
Take one away from the major seventh.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A major seventh is 11 semitones, and a minor seventh is one fewer, 10.

questions.onCorrect: A minor seventh is 10 semitones, and its inversion is a major second of 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a major seventh. Minor is one semitone smaller.
That is a major sixth. The seventh is one letter higher.

questions.prompt: Name the interval from G up to B♭, with its quality and number.
hints: Count the letters G, A, B: the number is 3.
The major third above G is B, which is 4 semitones.
questions.onCorrect: G to B♭ is 3 semitones, one fewer than the major third, so it is a minor third.

questions.prompt: What does an augmented fourth become when it is inverted? Give its quality and number.
hints: The numbers add up to 9.
Inverting swaps augmented and diminished.
The sizes add up to 12: 6 plus the answer.
questions.onCorrect: An augmented fourth of 6 semitones fits with a diminished fifth of 6, so this pair splits the octave exactly in half.

questions.prompt: A key signature has three sharps, on F, C and G. Which major key is it? You built its scale in an earlier lesson.
hints: Recall the scale you built earlier that needed three black keys, F♯, C♯ and G♯.
The scale uses F♯, C♯ and G♯.
questions.onCorrect: A major has F♯, C♯ and G♯, and the key is a semitone above the last sharp, G♯.

misconceptions.feedback: G major has one sharp, F sharp. A key with three sharps lies further along.
D major has two sharps, F sharp and C sharp. Adding G sharp gives the scale that starts on A.
E major has four sharps, on F, C, G and D. The key with three stops before D sharp is added.

questions.prompt: A key signature has four sharps, on F, C, G and D. Which major key is it?
hints: The last sharp is the leading tone, one step below the tonic.
The tonic is a semitone above the last sharp, D.
questions.onCorrect: The leading tone is a semitone below the tonic, so four sharps give E major.

misconceptions.feedback: D is the last sharp, which is the leading tone. The key is a semitone above it.
G major has just one sharp. Count how many the signature has.
A major has three sharps. The signature here has four.

questions.prompt: How many flats does E♭ major have?
hints: Flats are added going down by fifths: C, F, B♭, E♭.
Count the steps from C to E♭ in that direction.
F is the first step, B♭ the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Going anticlockwise round the circle of fifths from C, F has 1 flat, B♭ has 2 and E♭ has 3.

questions.onCorrect: The flats of E♭ major are B♭, E♭ and A♭.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B♭ major. E♭ is one step further round.
That is A♭ major, one step beyond E♭.

questions.prompt: What is the relative minor of G major? Give the key, for example C minor.
hints: The relative key starts 3 semitones below the major tonic.
Count down 3 semitones from G.
questions.onCorrect: E minor shares the one sharp, F♯, with G major, and starts 3 semitones below G.

questions.prompt: Which major key has five flats, B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭ and G♭? Give the key in words, for example B flat major.
hints: With flats, the key is the second-to-last flat.
The flats in order are B, E, A, D, G.
questions.onCorrect: The last flat names the subdominant, and the one before it names the key, so five flats give D♭ major.

questions.prompt: Which major key has three flats, B♭, E♭ and A♭? Give the key in words, for example B flat major.
hints: The key is the second-to-last flat.
The flats are B, E, A.
questions.onCorrect: The second-to-last flat is E♭, and three flats give E♭ major.

questions.prompt: A key signature has two sharps. What is the relative minor of its major key? Give the key, for example C minor.
hints: Two sharps, F and C, give the major key D.
The relative minor starts 3 semitones below D.
questions.onCorrect: Two sharps give D major, and 3 semitones below D is B, so B minor.

questions.prompt: How many sharps does B major have?
hints: Count the steps up by fifths from C.
The keys are C, G, D, A, E, B.
G is the first step.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Going clockwise from C round the circle of fifths: G 1, D 2, A 3, E 4, B 5 sharps.

questions.onCorrect: The sharps are F, C, G, D and A, and B is a semitone above the last.

misconceptions.feedback: That is E major. B is one step further clockwise.
That is F♯ major, one step beyond B.

questions.prompt: Which major key has two flats? Give the key in words, for example E flat major.
hints: The key is the second-to-last flat.
The flats are B and E.
questions.onCorrect: With two flats, B♭ and E♭, the second-to-last is B♭, so the key is B♭ major.

questions.prompt: What is the relative minor of A major? Give the key in words, for example C minor.
hints: The relative minor starts 3 semitones below the major tonic.
Three semitones below A is a black key.
questions.onCorrect: F♯ minor shares A major's three sharps and starts 3 semitones below A.

questions.prompt: E natural minor is the relative minor of G major. How many sharps does it have?
hints: The relative minor uses the same signature as its relative major.
G major has F♯.
Count the sharps in G major.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: E natural minor shares G major's signature, which has one sharp, F♯.

questions.onCorrect: E natural minor is E, F♯, G, A, B, C, D, E.

misconceptions.feedback: That is A minor, the relative of C major. E minor goes with G major.
That is B minor, the relative of D major.

questions.prompt: In A natural minor the seventh note is G, a whole tone below the tonic A, while a major scale has a semitone at that point. Which note, a semitone below A, would lead into the tonic more strongly?
hints: Think of the leading tone of a major scale.
A semitone below A is G raised by a semitone.
questions.onCorrect: G♯ is a semitone below A, so it works as a leading tone, and raising the seventh degree gives harmonic minor.

misconceptions.feedback: G is a whole tone below A, which is the gap a leading tone closes. The note a semitone below A is G raised by a semitone.
F sharp is three semitones below A, further away than G. The note a semitone below A is the black key between G and A.
F is four semitones below A, further away than G. The note a semitone below A is the black key just under it.

questions.prompt: In C harmonic minor the sixth note is A♭ and the raised seventh is B. How many semitones lie between them?
hints: Count the keys from A♭ up to B, black and white.
A♭ to B♭ is a whole tone.
B is one more semitone above B♭.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A♭ to B♭ is 2 semitones and B♭ to B adds one, so A♭ to B is 3 semitones, an augmented second.

questions.onCorrect: The augmented second looks like a second on the staff but is as wide as a minor third.

misconceptions.feedback: That is A♭ to B♭, a whole tone. B is one semitone higher.
That is only the step from B♭ to B.

questions.prompt: What is the sixth note of D melodic minor going up? Give it in words, for example C sharp.
hints: Ascending melodic minor raises the sixth and seventh degrees of natural minor.
The sixth degree of D natural minor is B♭.
questions.onCorrect: Raising B♭ by a semitone gives B, and with C♯ above it the augmented second of harmonic minor is gone.

questions.prompt: How many sharps does B minor have?
hints: The relative major of B minor is a minor third above B.
That major key is D.
Count the sharps of D major.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: B minor shares its signature with D major, which has two sharps: F♯ and C♯.

questions.onCorrect: B minor is the relative minor of D major, while its parallel major, B major, has five sharps.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B major, the parallel major. A minor key takes the signature of its relative major, D major.
Three sharps belong to A major. Go up 3 semitones from B to find the relative major, D.

questions.prompt: Build G harmonic minor: G A B♭ C D E♭ and then the raised seventh. What is the seventh note? Give it in words, for example C sharp.
hints: The natural seventh note of G minor is F.
Raising it by a semitone gives the leading tone.
questions.onCorrect: F♯ is a semitone below G, and it sits 3 semitones above E♭, an augmented second.

questions.prompt: What is the seventh note of E harmonic minor? Give it in words, for example C sharp.
hints: E natural minor has F♯ and its seventh note is D.
Raise the seventh by a semitone.
questions.onCorrect: D♯ is the leading tone of E, a semitone below the tonic.

questions.prompt: What is the seventh note of B harmonic minor? Give it in words, for example G sharp.
hints: B natural minor has the seventh note A.
Harmonic minor raises the seventh by a semitone.
questions.onCorrect: A♯ is the leading tone of B, a semitone below the tonic.

questions.prompt: How many flats does F minor have?
hints: Go up 3 semitones from F to find the relative major.
That major key is A♭.
Count the flats of A♭ major.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F minor shares its signature with its relative major, A♭ major, which has four flats.

questions.onCorrect: F minor has B♭, E♭, A♭ and D♭.

misconceptions.feedback: That is C minor, whose relative major is E♭. F minor's relative major is A♭.
That is F major. F minor is the parallel key and has more flats.

questions.prompt: Which key is the parallel minor of C major?
hints: Parallel keys share a tonic.
The parallel minor of C major begins on C.
questions.onCorrect: C minor has three flats, while C major has none.

misconceptions.feedback: A minor is the relative minor. It shares C major's signature and has a different tonic.
E minor is the relative minor of G major.
G minor is the relative minor of B♭ major.

questions.prompt: A piece is played at 80 beats per minute. How many seconds does one beat last?
hints: There are 60 seconds in a minute.
Divide the seconds in a minute by the beats in a minute.
Work out 60 ÷ 80.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One beat lasts 60 ÷ 80 = 0.75 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: A faster tempo gives a shorter beat: at 120 per minute each beat lasts half a second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 80 ÷ 60. A beat is the time per beat, which is minutes divided into beats, so use 60 ÷ 80.
That is the beat at 75 per minute. Divide 60 by 80.

questions.prompt: A quarter note lasts one beat, and a dot after a note adds half of the note's own length. How long does a dotted quarter note last?
hints: The dot adds half of the length of the note it follows.
Half of one beat is half a beat.
Add it to the note's own length.
questions.onCorrect: A dotted half note lasts 3 beats by the same rule.

misconceptions.feedback: That would add a whole beat. The dot adds only half of the note's own length.
That would add a quarter of a beat. The dot adds half the note's value, which for a quarter note is half a beat.
Half a beat is what the dot adds. It is added to the quarter note's own beat.

questions.prompt: How many sixteenth notes equal one dotted quarter note?
hints: Count how many sixteenth notes fill a quarter note.
A quarter note is 4 sixteenth notes.
The dot adds half of the 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A quarter note equals 4 sixteenth notes and the dot adds half of that, 2 more, so a dotted quarter equals 6 sixteenths.

questions.onCorrect: A dotted quarter note is 1.5 beats, and 1.5 × 4 = 6 sixteenth notes.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds only one sixteenth. The dot adds half of the 4 sixteenths in a quarter.
That is a half note, which is twice a quarter. A dotted quarter is 1.5 times it.

questions.prompt: How is a bar of 6/8 usually felt?
hints: The notes are grouped by the beaming.
Each beat divides into three.

acceptedIdeas: two beats, each of three eighth notes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: two beats, each of three eighth notes

questions.onCorrect: Each beat in 6/8 is a dotted quarter note, so the bar has two beats.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every eighth note as a beat. In 6/8 they are grouped, so the beat is longer.
That is how 3/4 feels when its quarters are split. In 6/8 the eighths are grouped in threes.
Six eighths would then have no internal pulse. They fall into two groups of three.

choices.label: two beats, each of three eighth notes
six beats of one eighth each
three beats, each of two eighth notes

questions.prompt: A bar of 4/4 holds a quarter note, an eighth note, two quarter notes and an eighth note, so notes begin at the points 1, 2, the & after 2, the & after 3 and the & after 4. How many notes begin exactly on a beat, 1, 2, 3 or 4?
hints: List where each note starts, and compare with the beat numbers.
The beats are the numbers and the & falls between them.
Check the opening note, then each note that follows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first two notes begin on beats 1 and 2. The other three begin on an & between beats.

questions.onCorrect: The notes that start on the & after 2 and after 3 are held across beats 3 and 4, so those beats pass with no new note, which is what makes the second half of the bar syncopated.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every note. Most of them begin on an &, which is not a beat.
That counts the beats in the bar, not the notes that start on them.

questions.prompt: A piece in 3/4 is played at 90 beats per minute. How many seconds does one bar last?
hints: Find the length of one beat first.
One beat is 60 ÷ 90 seconds, and the top number gives the beats in a bar.
Multiply by 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One beat lasts 60 ÷ 90 = 2/3 of a second, and a bar of 3/4 has 3 beats, so a bar lasts 3 × 2/3 = 2 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: A bar of 3/4 at 90 beats per minute lasts 2 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one beat. A bar of 3/4 has three of them.
That is 3 beats at one second each. At 90 per minute a beat is shorter.

questions.prompt: At 120 beats per minute the beat is a quarter note. How many seconds does one eighth note last?
hints: Find the length of a quarter note first.
An eighth note is half a quarter note.
Halve 0.5 seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At 120 per minute a quarter note lasts 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 seconds, and an eighth note is half of that, 0.25 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: Eighth notes at 120 per minute come four to the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a whole quarter-note beat. An eighth is half of it.
That is a sixteenth note. An eighth is twice as long.

questions.prompt: At 75 beats per minute, how many seconds does one bar of 4/4 last?
hints: Find the length of one beat first.
One beat is 60 ÷ 75 seconds, and a bar of 4/4 has four beats.
Multiply by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One beat lasts 60 ÷ 75 = 0.8 seconds, and a bar of 4/4 has 4 beats, so it lasts 4 × 0.8 = 3.2 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: At 75 per minute, 20 bars of 4/4 take a little over a minute.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one beat. A bar of 4/4 has four of them.
That uses 60 ÷ 75 incorrectly as 1.2. A beat is 60 ÷ 75 = 0.8 seconds.

questions.prompt: In 4/4, how many beats does a dotted half note last?
hints: A half note lasts two quarter-note beats.
The dot adds half of two beats.
Add that to 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A half note lasts 2 beats and the dot adds half of that, 1 beat, so a dotted half note lasts 3 beats.

questions.onCorrect: A dotted half note fills three-quarters of a bar of 4/4.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds half a beat. The dot adds half of the note's own 2 beats.
That is a whole note, which fills the bar.

questions.prompt: In a time signature of 3/4, what does the bottom number 4 tell you?
hints: The top number counts beats in a bar.
The bottom number names a kind of note.

acceptedIdeas: each beat is a quarter note
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: each beat is a quarter note

questions.onCorrect: So 3/4 is three quarter-note beats in each bar.

misconceptions.feedback: The number of beats is the top number. The bottom number names the note that gets one beat.
The time signature says nothing about seconds. That depends on the tempo.
Tempo is a separate marking. The bottom number names a note value.

choices.label: the tempo is four beats a minute
there are four beats in the bar
each beat is a quarter note

questions.prompt: Stacking thirds on D using only the notes of C major gives D, F, A. In C, E, G the lower third, C up to E, is 4 semitones. How does the lower third of D, F, A compare?
hints: Count each key from D to F, black and white.
E and F touch.
The keys above D are D♯, E, F.
questions.onCorrect: So a chord on D built from the white keys has a smaller lower third than the chord on C.

misconceptions.feedback: D up to F passes D sharp and E, and E and F touch, so it has fewer semitones than C up to E, not more.
Both skip one white key, but between D and F the keys E and F touch, so there is one black key fewer than between C and E.
Two semitones smaller would be a whole tone, D up to E. F is one semitone above E, so D up to F is 3 semitones.

choices.label: The same, since both skip one white key

questions.prompt: Name the notes of an F major triad, in order from the root, for example C E G.
hints: Stack thirds on F by skipping a letter each time: F, then A, then C.
Check: F to A should be 4 semitones and A to C should be 3.
questions.onCorrect: F A C has a major third of 4 semitones below a minor third of 3, so it is major.

questions.prompt: In E major, the chord C♯ E G♯ has which Roman numeral?
hints: The numeral names the scale degree of the root.
Count up the E major scale to C♯: E F♯ G♯ A B C♯.
questions.onCorrect: C♯ E G♯ is a minor triad on the sixth degree, so its numeral is a small vi.

misconceptions.feedback: iii is the chord on the third degree, G♯. The chord here starts on C♯.
ii is the chord on the second degree, F♯.
IV is the chord on the fourth degree, A.

questions.prompt: How many semitones separate the root and the fifth of a diminished triad?
hints: A diminished triad is 3 + 3.
Add the two stacked thirds.
Both are minor thirds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A diminished triad stacks a minor third and a minor third, 3 + 3 = 6 semitones from root to fifth.

questions.onCorrect: That span of 6 semitones is a diminished fifth, which is where the name comes from.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the root-to-fifth distance of a major or minor triad. A diminished triad's fifth is one semitone smaller.
That is an augmented triad, 4 + 4.

questions.prompt: D7 contains the notes D F♯ A C. How many semitones are there from D up to C?
hints: The seventh in a dominant seventh chord is a minor seventh.
A major seventh is 11 semitones.
A minor seventh is one fewer.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: D to C is a minor seventh: a major seventh would be 11, so the minor seventh is 10 semitones.

questions.onCorrect: That minor seventh above the root is what separates the dominant seventh from a major seventh chord.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a major seventh, D up to C♯.
That is a major sixth.

questions.prompt: The notes F, A and C are played with C as the lowest note. In what position is this chord? Give the inversion.
hints: The chord is F major, with F as its root.
Root position has the root lowest, and the inversion is named by which chord note is lowest.
Decide whether C is the root, the third or the fifth of the chord.
questions.onCorrect: C is the fifth of F major, so with C lowest the chord is still F major, in second inversion.

questions.prompt: Build the triad on the sixth degree of A major. Counting thirds, it is F♯ A C♯. What is its quality? Give the quality word.
hints: F♯ to A is 3 semitones and A to C♯ is 4.
A smaller third at the bottom gives a particular quality.
questions.onCorrect: 3 + 4 is a minor triad, so the chord is F♯ minor and its numeral is a small vi.

questions.prompt: D major has the notes D E F♯ G A B C♯. What is the quality of the triad on its seventh degree, C♯ E G?
hints: C♯ to E is 3 semitones, and E to G is also 3.
Two minor thirds stacked give a particular quality.
questions.onCorrect: The triad on the seventh degree of any major scale is diminished, which is why it is written with a small numeral and a degree sign.

questions.prompt: How many semitones separate the root and the fifth of an augmented triad?
hints: An augmented triad is 4 + 4.
Add the two stacked thirds.
Both are major thirds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: An augmented triad stacks two major thirds, 4 + 4 = 8 semitones from root to fifth.

questions.onCorrect: That span of 8 semitones is an augmented fifth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a major or minor triad's root to fifth. An augmented fifth is one semitone more.
That is a diminished triad, 3 + 3.

questions.prompt: Name the notes of an F minor triad, in order from the root, for example C E G.
hints: Stack thirds from F, skipping a letter each time.
F to A is 4 semitones, so the minor third above F is A lowered by a semitone.
questions.onCorrect: F A♭ C is 3 semitones then 4, which makes a minor triad.

questions.prompt: In D major, what is the Roman numeral of the chord E G B?
hints: E is the second note of the D major scale.
E G B is 3 + 4 semitones, a minor triad.
questions.onCorrect: A minor triad on the second degree is written with a small numeral, ii, in D major as in every major key.

questions.prompt: B is the seventh degree of C major. How many semitones is it below the tonic C?
hints: B and C are neighbours on the keyboard.
Is there a black key between them?
Count the keys from B up to C.
questions.onCorrect: That semitone is why the seventh degree is called the leading tone: it leads up into the tonic.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be a whole tone, as from B flat to C. The white keys B and C touch.
3 semitones is the distance from A up to C. B and C are neighbouring keys.
5 semitones is the distance from G up to C. B is much closer to C than that.

questions.prompt: A7, the dominant seventh of D major, has the notes A, C♯, E and G. How many semitones lie between its third, C♯, and its seventh, G?
hints: Count each key from C♯ up to G, black and white.
E to F is a semitone, with no black key between.
The keys above C♯ are D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: C♯ up to G passes D, D♯, E, F and F♯ and lands on G: 6 semitones, a tritone, just as B to F is in G7.

questions.onCorrect: Every dominant seventh holds a tritone between its third and its seventh, which is why every V7 pulls toward its tonic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is C♯ up to F♯, a perfect fourth. Count on to G.
That is a perfect fifth, C♯ up to G♯. G itself is one semitone lower.

questions.prompt: In F major, what is the V chord? Name its root.
hints: V is the chord on the fifth note of the scale.
F major is F, G, A, B♭, C, D, E.
questions.onCorrect: C E G is a major triad, as every V chord in a major key is.

questions.prompt: A phrase in G major ends with a D major chord followed by an E minor chord. What is this cadence called?
hints: Work out the numerals of D major and E minor in G major.
V followed by vi sets up the expected tonic and then substitutes another chord.
questions.onCorrect: D is V and E minor is vi in G major, and vi shares two notes with I, so the move sounds close but surprising.

questions.prompt: A phrase in F major ends on a C major chord, pausing without arriving home. Which cadence is this?
hints: Work out which degree of F major C is.
Only one cadence ends on V.
questions.onCorrect: A half cadence leaves the phrase open, a bit like a comma.

misconceptions.feedback: An authentic cadence goes from V to I, so it ends on the tonic.
A plagal cadence goes from IV to I and ends on the tonic.
A deceptive cadence goes from V to vi, so it ends on vi.

questions.prompt: In E major, the progression I V vi IV starts on E and B. Which chord is vi? Name it, for example D minor.
hints: The vi chord is built on the sixth degree.
The sixth note of E major is C♯, and the triad on it is 3 + 4 semitones.
questions.onCorrect: vi is always the relative minor of I, so in E major it is C♯ minor.

questions.prompt: In B♭ major, what is the vi chord? Give its name, for example D minor.
hints: The sixth note of B♭ major is G.
vi is a minor triad.
questions.onCorrect: G minor is the relative minor of B♭ major, and shares its signature of B♭ and E♭.

questions.prompt: When A7 resolves to D, C♯ rises to D and G falls to F♯. How many semitones lie between D and F♯?
hints: Count the keys from D up to F♯.
D to E is 2 and E to F♯ is 2.
Add the two steps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: D up to F♯ is 4 semitones, a major third, so the tritone of 6 semitones has closed to 4.

questions.onCorrect: The two notes of the tritone move inward and end a major third apart.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the tritone C♯ to G before it resolves. After resolving, the notes are D and F♯.
That is a minor third, D to F.

questions.prompt: In B major, what is the IV chord? Name its root.
hints: Count up the B major scale: B, C♯, D♯, E.
IV is the chord on the fourth degree.
questions.onCorrect: The IV chord of B major is E G♯ B, a major triad.

questions.prompt: Which cadence is the move from IV to I?
hints: Name the cadences by their last two chords.
Only one has IV as its first chord.
questions.onCorrect: A plagal cadence is the soft close often sung on the word Amen at the end of a hymn.

misconceptions.feedback: An authentic cadence is V to I, not IV to I.
A half cadence ends on V.
A deceptive cadence goes from V to vi.

questions.prompt: A bass note C3 and a tenor note G3 sound together. What interval do they make?
hints: Count the letter names from C up to G, with C as 1.
Then count the semitones from C up to G and compare them with the major scale.
questions.onCorrect: A perfect fifth like this is one of the two intervals that parallel motion is not allowed to repeat.

misconceptions.feedback: A major third is C up to E, 4 semitones. C up to G spans five letter names and 7 semitones.
A perfect fourth is C up to F, 5 semitones. G is one letter further on.
An octave above C3 is C4. G3 is five letter names up from C3, 7 semitones.

questions.prompt: The soprano moves from E5 to F5 while the bass moves from C3 down to A2. What is this motion?
hints: Does each voice move up or down?
Compare the two directions.
questions.onCorrect: Contrary motion keeps the voices independent, and it is the safest way to approach a perfect interval.

misconceptions.feedback: In parallel motion both voices move the same way and keep the same interval. Here one rises and one falls.
In similar motion both voices move in the same direction. Here they move in opposite directions.
In oblique motion one voice holds. Both voices move here.

questions.prompt: The tenor moves from A3 to B3 while the bass moves from D3 to E3. What is the problem?
hints: Measure the interval between the voices at each chord.
Check which way both voices move.
questions.onCorrect: Both voices rise a step together while staying a fifth apart, which sounds like a single voice doubled.

misconceptions.feedback: The notes are D and A, a fifth apart, and E and B, a fifth apart. An octave would be the same letter name.
The tenor stays above the bass throughout, so the voices do not cross.
Both pairs are perfect fifths and both voices rise, which is exactly what is avoided.

questions.prompt: The tenor is moved from A3 down to F3 to fix the parallel fifths, and the bass is on D3. How many semitones are there from D3 up to F3?
hints: Count each key from D up to F.
E and F touch on the keyboard.
The keys above D are D♯, E, F.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: D3 up to F3 passes D♯ and E and lands on F: 3 semitones, a minor third. The fifth has become a third.

questions.onCorrect: The voices now move in contrary motion, and the interval between them changes from a fifth to a third.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a major third, D up to F♯.
That is D up to E, a whole tone.

questions.prompt: In the move from C major to F major, the bass is on F3 and the tenor is on A3. How many semitones are there from F3 up to A3?
hints: Count each key from F up to A.
F to G is a whole tone.
G to A is a whole tone.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F3 up to A3 passes F♯, G and G♯ and lands on A: 4 semitones, a major third. The earlier fifth C to G has become a third, so there are no parallel fifths.

questions.onCorrect: A major third is not a perfect interval, so the rule about parallels does not apply to it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is F up to A♭, a minor third. A is a whole tone above G.
That is the earlier fifth, C up to G. The bass has moved to F.

questions.prompt: In G major the leading tone is F♯. To which note does it resolve in V7 to I? Give the letter.
hints: The leading tone rises by a semitone.
It resolves to the tonic.
questions.onCorrect: F♯ rises a semitone to G, the tonic of the key.

questions.prompt: Two voices move so that one holds its note while the other moves. What kind of motion is this?
hints: Both parallel and similar need both voices to move.
Contrary needs both voices to move in opposite directions.
questions.onCorrect: Oblique motion is the gentlest way to change harmony, since it keeps one note fixed.

questions.prompt: The soprano moves from D5 to E5 while the alto moves from G4 to A4. What is the problem? Name it.
hints: Measure the interval between the voices at each chord.
G up to D is 7 semitones.
questions.onCorrect: Both pairs are perfect fifths and both voices rise.

questions.prompt: Which note does the leading tone B resolve to in C major? Give the letter.
hints: The leading tone is a semitone below the tonic.
It rises.
questions.onCorrect: B rises a semitone to C, while the seventh of V7, F, falls to E.

questions.prompt: In an eight-bar period in F major, the first phrase ends on a C major chord. What cadence closes this first phrase?
hints: Work out which degree of F major C is.
Cadences were named in the progressions lesson.
questions.onCorrect: The antecedent leaves the harmony open, and the consequent answers it by closing on I.

questions.prompt: What form is ABACADA?
hints: The main section A returns after each contrasting section.
Look at what keeps coming back between the new sections.
questions.onCorrect: A rondo can have more than two contrasting sections, and here the main theme A is heard four times, with B, C and D between.

questions.prompt: A twelve-bar blues is in 4/4, so each bar holds four beats. How many beats does one time through the pattern contain?
hints: The top number of 4/4 gives the beats in a bar.
Multiply by the number of bars in the blues.
Work out 12 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: Counting bars gives 12 and counting beats gives 48, which are different questions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of bars. Each bar has four beats.
That is 4 × 4, a single row of four bars. The blues has three rows.
144 is 12 × 12. Each bar of 4/4 has 4 beats, not 12.

questions.prompt: In a twelve-bar blues in F, which chord plays in bar 9? Name its root.
hints: Bars 9 and 10 are V and IV.
V in F major is the chord on the fifth degree.
questions.onCorrect: Bar 9 is the V chord, which gives the third row its pull back toward home.

questions.prompt: In a sonata-form piece in C major, where does the second theme return in the recapitulation?
hints: Look at which key the exposition's second theme left.
The piece has to end where it began.
questions.onCorrect: The recapitulation brings the second theme into the home key, which resolves the key tension created in the exposition.

misconceptions.feedback: That is where it sat in the exposition. Moving it to the home key is the point of the recapitulation.
The second theme comes home to the key of the piece, not to its relative minor.
Both themes return in the recapitulation.

choices.label: in the relative minor, A minor

questions.prompt: A twelve-bar blues in 4/4 is played at 120 beats per minute. How many seconds does one chorus last?
hints: Find the length of one beat first.
A bar of 4/4 has four beats, so find the length of a bar.
Multiply the length of a bar by the number of bars.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One beat lasts 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5 seconds, a bar has 4 beats, so 2 seconds, and 12 bars last 12 × 2 = 24 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: At 120 beats per minute each bar lasts 2 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of beats. Multiply by the length of a beat, 0.5 seconds.
That counts one second per bar. A bar of 4 beats at 120 per minute lasts 2 seconds.

questions.prompt: In a twelve-bar blues in A, which chord plays in bar 9? Name its root.
hints: Bar 9 is the V chord.
The fifth note of A major is E.
questions.onCorrect: V in A major is E, so the third row of the blues in A begins on E.

questions.prompt: Each section of a rondo in the form ABACA is 8 bars long. How many bars does the whole rondo have?
hints: Count the letters in ABACA, including repeats.
Each letter stands for a section of 8 bars.
Multiply the number of sections by 8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ABACA has 5 sections and 5 × 8 = 40 bars.

questions.onCorrect: The A section is played three times, so it accounts for 24 of the 40 bars.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the A sections, which return three times. B and C add two more sections.
That counts only the sections with different letters, A, B and C, plus one.

questions.prompt: A twelve-bar blues in 4/4 is played at 90 beats per minute. How many seconds does one chorus last?
hints: Count the beats in the whole chorus first.
Each beat lasts 60 divided by the tempo.
Multiply the beats by the length of a beat.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chorus has 12 × 4 = 48 beats, and each beat lasts 60 ÷ 90 of a second, so 48 × 60 ÷ 90 = 32 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: At 90 beats per minute a chorus of 48 beats takes 32 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of beats. Each lasts less than a second at 90 per minute.
That is the answer at 120 beats per minute.

questions.prompt: What form is ABA, in which the first section returns after a contrasting one?
hints: The form has three sections.
The word means made of three.
questions.onCorrect: Ternary form is three parts: a statement, a contrast and a return.

questions.prompt: In a twelve-bar blues in D, which chord plays in bar 5? Name its root.
hints: Bar 5 begins the second row.
The second row starts on IV.
questions.onCorrect: Bar 5 is the IV chord, G in the key of D.

flashcards.front: How many semitones are there in an octave?
flashcards.back: Twelve: seven white keys and five black keys per octave, each a step.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Twelve: seven white keys and five black keys per octave, each a step.

flashcards.front: A4 is 440 Hz. What is the frequency of A5 in Hz?
flashcards.back: One octave up doubles the frequency: 880 Hz.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One octave up doubles the frequency: 880 Hz.

flashcards.front: Why is going from 440 Hz to 660 Hz not an octave?
flashcards.back: An octave is a doubling, so the ratio matters; 660 ÷ 440 = 1.5, which is a fifth.

flashcards.front: Which letter does the bass clef mark, with its two dots on either side of that line?
flashcards.back: The dots surround the fourth line, which is F3, so the bass clef is also the F clef.

flashcards.front: What is the name of the lowest line of the treble staff?
flashcards.back: The bottom line of the treble staff is E4, and the lines go E, G, B, D, F upward.

flashcards.front: Why can the same pitch be written in both the treble staff and the bass staff?
flashcards.back: A clef only says which line is which pitch, so middle C appears below the treble staff or above the bass staff and sounds the same.

flashcards.front: What do we call a step of two semitones?
flashcards.back: A whole tone is two semitones, as between C and D, where a black key sits in between.

flashcards.front: What is another name for the key D♯, in words, for example F sharp?
flashcards.back: D♯ is one semitone above D, and E♭ is one semitone below E, so both name the same black key.

flashcards.front: How many semitones does the chromatic scale contain between one note and the same note an octave higher?
flashcards.back: The chromatic scale uses every key, so it takes twelve semitone steps to span an octave.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chromatic scale uses every key, so it takes twelve semitone steps to span an octave.

flashcards.front: What is the step pattern of the major scale, using W for a whole tone and H for a half step?
flashcards.back: The steps are W W H W W W H, with half steps between degrees 3 and 4 and 7 and 8.

acceptedIdeas: W W H W W W H
acceptedAlternatives: W W H W W W H
whole whole half whole whole whole half
w w h w w w h
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: W W H W W W H

flashcards.front: What is the first note of a scale, the one it is named after, called?
flashcards.back: The first note is the tonic, and the scale is named after it.

flashcards.front: What is the seventh note of a major scale, a semitone below the tonic, called?
flashcards.back: The leading tone sits a semitone under the tonic and pulls toward it.

flashcards.front: How many semitones are there in a major third?
flashcards.back: A major third has 4 semitones, which is the third degree of a major scale above the tonic.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A major third has 4 semitones, which is the third degree of a major scale above the tonic.

flashcards.front: How many semitones are there in a perfect fifth?
flashcards.back: A perfect fifth has 7 semitones, the distance from the tonic to the dominant.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A perfect fifth has 7 semitones, the distance from the tonic to the dominant.

flashcards.front: Why do C up to G♭ and C up to F♯ have different names though they are the same size?
flashcards.back: The number counts letters, so G♭ makes a fifth and F♯ makes a fourth, and both are 6 semitones.

flashcards.front: In what order do the sharps appear in a key signature, from the first? Give the letters.
flashcards.back: Each new sharp is a perfect fifth above the last, giving F C G D A E B.

acceptedIdeas: F C G D A E B
acceptedAlternatives: F C G D A E B
f c g d a e b
F, C, G, D, A, E, B
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: F C G D A E B

flashcards.front: A signature has sharps. How do you find the key from the last sharp?
flashcards.back: The last sharp is the leading tone, so the key is one semitone above it.

acceptedIdeas: a semitone above the last sharp
acceptedAlternatives: a semitone above the last sharp
one semitone above the last sharp
a half step above the last sharp
half step above the last sharp
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: a semitone above the last sharp

flashcards.front: Why does going up a fifth on the circle add one sharp?
flashcards.back: A new fifth above the tonic shifts the scale so one new note is a semitone higher, which is one more sharp.

flashcards.front: Which degree does harmonic minor raise compared with natural minor?
flashcards.back: The seventh degree is raised by a semitone so that it leads to the tonic.

flashcards.front: What step pattern gives natural minor, using W and H?
flashcards.back: Natural minor goes W H W W H W W, starting from the tonic.

acceptedIdeas: W H W W H W W
acceptedAlternatives: W H W W H W W
whole half whole whole half whole whole
w h w w h w w
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: W H W W H W W

flashcards.front: What is the difference between the relative and the parallel minor of a major key?
flashcards.back: The relative minor shares the signature and has a different tonic, while the parallel minor shares the tonic and has a different signature.

flashcards.front: A quarter note lasts one beat. How many beats does a half note last?
flashcards.back: A half note is twice a quarter note, so it lasts two beats.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A half note is twice a quarter note, so it lasts two beats.

flashcards.front: At 60 beats per minute, how many seconds does one beat last?
flashcards.back: 60 beats take 60 seconds, so each beat lasts one second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60 beats take 60 seconds, so each beat lasts one second.

flashcards.front: Why is 6/8 felt as two beats and not six?
flashcards.back: The six eighth notes group in threes, so each group of three is one beat, a dotted quarter.

flashcards.front: What two thirds, in semitones, make a major triad?
flashcards.back: A major triad is a major third of 4 semitones plus a minor third of 3 semitones.

flashcards.front: In a major key, which triads are minor? Give the Roman numerals.
flashcards.back: The triads on the second, third and sixth degrees are minor, written ii, iii and vi.

flashcards.front: Why does a chord keep its name when its lowest note changes?
flashcards.back: The name comes from the stack of thirds above the root, so playing the same notes with another one lowest gives an inversion of the same chord.

flashcards.front: In a major key, which two chords usually have a dominant function? Give the Roman numerals.
flashcards.back: V and vii° have a dominant function, since both contain the leading tone.

flashcards.front: What is the cadence V to I called?
flashcards.back: The authentic cadence moves from V to I and is the strongest close.

flashcards.front: Why does V7 pull toward I?
flashcards.back: Its leading tone B rises a semitone to C and its seventh F falls a semitone to E, so the tritone resolves inward.

flashcards.front: Two voices move in the same direction by the same interval. What is this motion called?
flashcards.back: Parallel motion keeps the interval between the voices the same, such as two voices a third apart both rising.

flashcards.front: Which two intervals must not appear in parallel in four-part writing? Give the interval names.
flashcards.back: Perfect fifths and perfect octaves moving in parallel make two voices sound like one.

flashcards.front: Why is it good to keep a note that two chords share in the same voice?
flashcards.back: A voice that holds its note moves no distance at all, so the join between the chords is smooth.

flashcards.front: How many bars are there in the standard blues, counting one chorus?
flashcards.back: The standard blues is twelve bars long, in three rows of four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The standard blues is twelve bars long, in three rows of four.

flashcards.front: What are the two phrases of a period called?
flashcards.back: The first is the antecedent, which ends on a weaker cadence, and the second is the consequent, which ends on a stronger one.

flashcards.front: Why does the second theme come back in the home key in a recapitulation?
flashcards.back: The exposition moved to a new key, creating tension, and the recapitulation resolves it by bringing everything back home.
